  • ELO-071: Describe the siting requirements for VHF line-of-sight (LOS) communications.
  • ELO-072: Secure guy ropes and anchors.
Body

OE-254 Component Identification

Before assembly, the operator must inventory the OE-254 kit to ensure all mission-essential parts are present and functional.

  • Base Stake and Base Plate: Provides the foundation and grounding for the mast.
  • Mast Sections: Interlocking tubular sections that provide the required height for LOS.
  • Bicone Assembly: The radiating element consisting of the feedcone and elements.
  • Guy Ropes and Anchors: Used to stabilize the mast against wind and weight.
  • Coaxial Cable (RG-213): Connects the antenna to the radio set.

VHF Siting and Signal Propagation

VHF signals (30-300 MHz) primarily travel via line-of-sight. The physical environment directly impacts signal reliability.

  • Terrain: High ground is preferred to clear the curvature of the earth and physical obstacles.
  • Vegetation: Heavy foliage can absorb VHF signals; antennas should be cleared of immediate brush or raised above the canopy.
  • Man-made Obstacles: Avoid power lines and large metal structures which cause signal reflection or interference.

Erection and Guying Procedures

Structural stability is achieved through proper guying. Per MCRP 3-40.3C, the mast must be secured to prevent collapse and ensure safety.

  • Guying Intervals: Guy ropes must be spaced at 120-degree intervals around the mast.
  • Anchor Placement: Anchors should be driven into the ground at a distance from the base equal to approximately 1/2 to 2/3 of the mast height.
  • Tensioning: Ropes must be taut but not over-tightened to avoid bowing the mast sections.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your platoon has established a patrol base in a wooded area. You are tasked with erecting an OE-254 to establish a VHF link with the Company Command Post located 15km away.

Practice Steps:

  1. Conduct a layout and inventory of the OE-254 kit.
  2. Select a site that maximizes elevation and minimizes foliage interference.
  3. Assemble the bicone and attach the coaxial cable.
  4. Connect mast sections and raise the antenna.
  5. Drive anchors and secure guy ropes at 120-degree intervals.
  6. Perform a radio check to verify signal strength.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the identification of the OE-254 kit, the critical nature of VHF line-of-sight siting, and the technical standards for securing the mast with 120-degree guying.

Closing Statement: The OE-254 is a force multiplier. When you master its assembly and siting, you ensure that your commander's intent can be heard across the battlefield, regardless of the terrain.

Lesson 28: Planning the Antenna Farm Layout

TLO: TLO-028

Introduction

Gain Attention: A poorly planned antenna farm is a beacon for enemy Direction Finding (DF) and a self-inflicted wound of signal interference. If your antennas are too close, your radios will 'talk' to each other instead of the distant end. To keep our communications secure and clear, we must plan our layouts with mathematical precision.

Overview: This lesson focuses on the tactical and technical considerations for antenna farm placement, the principles of mutual interference, and the calculation of separation distances to ensure electromagnetic compatibility.

Objectives:

  • TLO-028: Plan the layout of an antenna farm.
  • ELO-073: Identify siting considerations for an antenna farm.
  • ELO-074: Explain the principles of mutual interference.
  • ELO-075: Determine minimum separation distances between antennas.
Body

Siting Considerations

Planning an antenna farm requires balancing three primary categories of considerations per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 8.

  • Doctrinal: Proximity to the Command Post (CP) and accessibility for operators.
  • Tactical: Use of natural concealment (reverse slopes) and security from enemy ground observation.
  • Technical: Soil conductivity for grounding and clear paths for signal propagation.

Mutual Interference Principles

Mutual interference occurs when multiple transmitters operate in close proximity, degrading the performance of nearby receivers.

  • Cosite Interference: When a transmitter desensitizes a receiver on a different frequency due to physical proximity.
  • Frequency Separation: The requirement to maintain a minimum 'buffer' between assigned frequencies to prevent bleed-over.
  • Harmonics: Secondary signals generated at multiples of the fundamental frequency that can interfere with other nets.

Antenna Separation and Layout

To mitigate interference, antennas must be physically separated based on their operating characteristics.

  • Horizontal Separation: The physical distance between masts; generally, the further the better, but limited by cable length.
  • Vertical Separation: Placing antennas at different heights to reduce coupling.
  • Polarization: Using different polarizations (vertical vs. horizontal) can provide up to 20dB of isolation.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are the Comm Chief for a Battalion Main CP. You have five VHF nets and two HF nets that must be operational within a 100m x 100m area. You must create a layout that prevents cosite interference.

Practice Steps:

  1. Analyze the frequency list to identify potential interference pairs.
  2. Determine the minimum horizontal separation distances based on frequency bands.
  3. Plot the antenna locations on a site overlay, considering terrain and concealment.
  4. Designate cable runs to avoid power line interference.
  5. Submit the completed antenna farm diagram for approval.
Conclusion

Summary: We have discussed the tactical and technical requirements for siting, the dangers of mutual interference, and the methods for determining proper antenna separation.

Closing Statement: Effective antenna farm planning ensures that our electronic signature is managed and our internal communications remain crystal clear. Plan with the enemy's DF capability in mind, and execute with technical discipline.

Lesson 29: Antenna Length Calculation

TLO: TLO-029

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are in a deep reconnaissance hide site and your primary whip antenna snaps. You have a spool of copper wire and a radio, but without the exact mathematical length for your assigned frequency, your signal will never reach the Combat Operations Center. Precision in antenna length is the difference between a successful CASEVAC call and total radio silence.

Overview: This lesson covers the mathematical requirements for determining the physical length of half-wave dipole and quarter-wave vertical antennas using standard military formulas found in MCRP 3-40.3C.

Objectives:

  • TLO-029: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole or quarter-wave vertical antenna.
  • ELO-076: State the mathematical formula for calculating the length of a half-wave dipole.
  • ELO-077: Calculate the length of a single leg of a half-wave dipole.
Body

The Standard Antenna Formula

To achieve resonance, an antenna must be cut to a specific fraction of the wavelength of the operating frequency. MCRP 3-40.3C provides constant values to simplify this calculation.

  • For feet: 468 divided by the frequency in MHz (468/f).
  • For meters: 143 divided by the frequency in MHz (143/f).
  • These constants account for the 'end effect' where the velocity of propagation is slightly slower in wire than in free space.

Calculating Half-Wave Dipole Total Length

The half-wave dipole is the most common field-expedient antenna. The formula provides the total length of the radiating element.

  • Example: For 7.0 MHz in feet: 468 / 7.0 = 66.85 feet.
  • Example: For 7.0 MHz in meters: 143 / 7.0 = 20.42 meters.

Calculating Individual Leg Lengths

A center-fed half-wave dipole consists of two distinct 'legs' or elements. To construct the antenna, the total length must be divided by two.

  • Formula: (Total Length) / 2 = Individual Leg Length.
  • Using the 7.0 MHz example: 66.85 feet / 2 = 33.42 feet per leg.
  • Accuracy is critical; MCRP 3-40.3C standards require precision within +/- 1 inch to maintain a low Standing Wave Ratio (SWR).
Practical Application

Scenario: You are the RTO for a platoon-sized patrol. Your frequency is 14.250 MHz. You must calculate the total length and individual leg lengths for a half-wave dipole in both feet and meters.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the frequency (14.250 MHz).
  2. Apply the formula for feet: 468 / 14.250.
  3. Apply the formula for meters: 143 / 14.250.
  4. Divide both results by 2 to determine the length of each individual wire leg.
  5. Record results on the calculation worksheet for instructor verification.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the standard formulas for antenna calculation (468/f and 143/f) and the process for determining both total and individual leg lengths for dipole antennas.

Closing Statement: Math is a weapon. By mastering these calculations, you ensure that your equipment is tuned to the exact frequency required to maintain the command and control link.

Lesson 30: Antenna Construction and Employment

TLO: TLO-030

Introduction

Gain Attention: A radio is simply a heavy box of electronics until it is connected to an efficient antenna system. In the field, you cannot rely on issued whips alone. Building a field-expedient dipole allows you to push your signal further, hide your signature, and overcome terrain obstacles that would stop other units in their tracks.

Overview: This lesson provides the technical skills to identify antenna components, understand the effects of polarization, and physically construct a resonant half-wave dipole antenna.

Objectives:

  • TLO-030: Demonstrate the construction and employment of a half-wave dipole antenna.
  • ELO-078: Identify the components of a field-expedient antenna system.
  • ELO-079: Describe the effects of antenna polarization and orientation.
  • ELO-080: Perform wire cutting and stripping for an antenna radiator.
Body

Components of the Dipole System

A standard field-expedient dipole consists of four primary components that must be properly integrated for the system to function.

  • Radiator: The wire elements cut to the specific frequency.
  • Insulators: Non-conductive materials at the ends and center to prevent signal grounding.
  • Transmission Line: Coaxial cable (e.g., RG-58) that carries the signal from the radio to the antenna.
  • Balun: A 'balanced-to-unbalanced' transformer used at the feed point to improve efficiency.

Polarization and Orientation

The physical orientation of the antenna determines the direction and 'shape' of the radio wave.

  • Horizontal Polarization: Antenna is parallel to the earth; best for long-range HF skywave and reducing man-made noise.
  • Vertical Polarization: Antenna is perpendicular to the earth; best for omni-directional ground wave communication.
  • Directivity: A horizontal dipole radiates energy best broadside (perpendicular) to the wire.

Construction Techniques

Proper mechanical construction ensures electrical reliability. Poorly stripped or loose wires create resistance and heat, which can damage the radio.

  • Measure twice, cut once: Always add 6-12 inches for 'pigtails' or tying off to insulators before cutting.
  • Stripping: Remove insulation without nicking the copper strands to prevent wire fatigue.
  • Strain Relief: Ensure the weight of the transmission line is supported by the center insulator, not the wire connections.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your team must establish a point-to-point HF link with a station 100 miles away. You have been provided with a frequency of 5.200 MHz, a spool of WD-1/TT wire, and two insulators.

Practice Steps:

  1. Calculate the required leg length for 5.200 MHz.
  2. Measure and cut two lengths of wire, adding 6 inches for attachment points.
  3. Strip 2 inches of insulation from the feed-point end of each wire.
  4. Attach the wires to the center and end insulators using a standard fisherman's knot or wire wrap.
  5. Connect the transmission line to the center feed point.
  6. Raise the antenna to a horizontal position at least 1/4 wavelength above the ground.
Conclusion

Summary: We have identified the components of the dipole, discussed how orientation affects your signal, and practiced the physical skills of cutting and stripping antenna wire.

Closing Statement: The ability to build an antenna from scrap wire is a hallmark of a professional communicator. Ensure your connections are tight and your measurements are exact.

Lesson 31: Employment and Assembly of the AS-2259/GR Antenna

TLO: TLO-031

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine your unit is operating in a deep mountain valley. Your standard vehicle whip antenna is failing to reach the Combat Operations Center (COC) because the signal is being blocked by the surrounding terrain. To get your message out, you need to shoot your signal straight up into the atmosphere so it can bounce back down over those mountains. This is the power of Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) and the AS-2259/GR antenna.

Overview: This lesson covers the identification of AS-2259/GR components, the principles of NVIS propagation, and the step-by-step assembly of the antenna system to support short-range HF communications.

Objectives:

  • TLO-031: Given an AS-2259/GR antenna kit, an HF radio, and a designated site, perform the assembly and erection of the AS-2259/GR antenna to support NVIS communications.
  • ELO-081: Identify the components of the AS-2259/GR antenna kit.
  • ELO-082: Explain the characteristics of Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation.
  • ELO-083: Assemble the mast and radiator elements of the AS-2259/GR.
Body

NVIS Propagation Principles

Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) is a technique used to establish reliable communications over distances of 0-300 miles, bypassing terrain obstacles.

  • Uses high take-off angles (near 90 degrees) to reflect signals off the ionosphere.
  • Requires specific frequency selection, typically between 2 and 12 MHz.
  • Eliminates the 'skip zone' common in standard HF skywave propagation.

AS-2259/GR Component Identification

The AS-2259/GR is a tactical, omnidirectional antenna designed specifically for NVIS.

  • Mast Sections: Seven interlocking sections that form the vertical support.
  • Top Mast Assembly: Contains the feed point for the radiator elements.
  • Radiator Elements: Two crossed-dipole wire assemblies that also serve as guy wires.
  • Base and Ground Stake: Provides stability and electrical grounding.

Assembly and Erection Procedures

Proper assembly ensures maximum signal radiation and structural integrity.

  • Site selection: Choose a level area clear of overhead obstructions.
  • Mast assembly: Ensure each section is fully seated to prevent collapse.
  • Radiator tensioning: Wire elements must be pulled taut at 90-degree intervals to maintain the 'crossed-dipole' configuration.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your team has been dropped at a remote patrol base in a canyon. You must establish an HF link back to the Battalion COC using the AS-2259/GR to overcome the terrain masking.

Practice Steps:

  1. Inventory the AS-2259/GR kit to ensure all components are present and serviceable.
  2. Layout the base and drive the ground stake into the center of the site.
  3. Assemble the mast sections and attach the top mast assembly.
  4. Deploy the radiator wires at 90-degree angles from each other.
  5. Erect the mast and secure the radiator wires to the ground stakes with proper tension.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the components of the AS-2259/GR, the theory of NVIS propagation for short-range HF, and the physical steps required to erect the system.

Closing Statement: Mastering the AS-2259/GR ensures that no matter the terrain, the Marine Corps maintains the ability to communicate and coordinate across the battlespace.

Lesson 32: Employment and Assembly of the OE-254 Antenna

TLO: TLO-032

Introduction

Gain Attention: In the VHF world, 'Height is Might.' If you are operating at the edge of your radio's range, every foot of elevation you gain can mean the difference between a clear transmission and total silence. The OE-254 allows you to put your antenna 30 feet in the air, significantly extending your Line of Sight (LOS) capabilities.

Overview: This lesson focuses on the OE-254 antenna system, including component identification, critical siting considerations for safety and performance, and the team-based guying and erection process.

Objectives:

  • TLO-032: Given an OE-254 antenna kit, a VHF radio, and a designated site, demonstrate the assembly and erection of the OE-254 antenna to its full height.
  • ELO-084: Identify the components of the OE-254 antenna kit.
  • ELO-085: Describe siting considerations for the OE-254 antenna.
  • ELO-086: Perform the guying of the OE-254 mast.
Body

OE-254 System Components

The OE-254 is a biconical, omnidirectional antenna designed for the 30-88 MHz VHF range.

  • Feed Cone and Radiating Elements: The 'top' of the antenna that handles the signal.
  • Mast Sections: Lightweight aluminum tubes used to reach the 30-foot height.
  • Guy Ropes and Plates: Used to stabilize the mast at two different levels.
  • Base Stake and Base Plate: The foundation of the mast system.

Siting and Safety Considerations

Because the OE-254 stands 30 feet tall and is made of conductive aluminum, site selection is a matter of both performance and life safety.

  • Line of Sight (LOS): Ensure the site is the highest available ground with minimal obstructions.
  • Power Line Safety: The antenna must be placed at a distance at least twice its height (60 feet) from any overhead power lines.
  • Grounding: Always use the provided ground stake to protect against static buildup and lightning.

Guying and Team Erection

Erecting a 30-foot mast requires a coordinated three-person team to prevent the mast from buckling or falling.

  • Guying Intervals: Secure guy ropes at 120-degree intervals (three directions).
  • Team Roles: One person on the mast, two people managing guy ropes to maintain verticality during the lift.
  • Tensioning: Ensure ropes are tight enough to withstand wind but not so tight they bend the aluminum mast.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your platoon is establishing a static observation post. You are tasked with erecting an OE-254 to ensure the VHF net remains reliable over the 15-mile distance to the company headquarters.

Practice Steps:

  1. Conduct a site survey to ensure clearance from power lines and optimal LOS.
  2. Assemble the feed cone and radiating elements on the ground.
  3. Connect the coaxial cable to the feed cone before raising the mast.
  4. Assemble the mast sections while the team members prepare the guy stakes at 120-degree intervals.
  5. Raise the antenna to its full 30-foot height using the three-person lift method, securing guys at each level.
Conclusion

Summary: We have identified the OE-254 components, discussed the critical safety distances from power lines, and practiced the team-based guying techniques required for a 30-foot erection.

Closing Statement: The OE-254 is a force multiplier for VHF communications. Erecting it quickly and safely ensures your unit stays connected when the distance gets long.

Lesson 33: Implementing Antenna Ground Systems

TLO: TLO-033

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are operating in a high-tempo environment where your signal is barely breaking the squelch of the receiving station. You have the right frequency and the right power setting, but your signal is still weak. The difference between mission success and communication failure might literally be beneath your feet. By properly implementing a ground system, you can reclaim lost energy and turn a marginal link into a crystal-clear circuit.

Overview: This lesson covers the theory and practical application of antenna ground systems, specifically focusing on how ground screens and counterpoises improve radiation efficiency for vertical whip antennas.

Objectives:

  • Explain the purpose of an antenna ground system per MCRP 3-40.3C.
  • Differentiate between a ground screen and a counterpoise per MCRP 3-40.3C.
  • Install a counterpoise system using four radial wires of the correct length per MCRP 3-40.3C.
Body

Purpose of Antenna Ground Systems

A ground system is essential for vertical antennas to provide a low-resistance return path for radio frequency (RF) energy. Without an adequate ground, energy is lost to the earth as heat rather than being radiated as a signal.

  • Reduces ground loss by providing a highly conductive path.
  • Improves radiation efficiency, ensuring more power reaches the distant station.
  • Acts as the 'other half' of the antenna system for unbalanced radiators like the vertical whip.

Ground Screen vs. Counterpoise

While both improve performance, they are utilized in different tactical scenarios based on the soil and the antenna height.

  • Ground Screen: A series of buried or surface-laid wires used to reduce resistance in the immediate vicinity of the antenna base.
  • Counterpoise: An artificial ground system used when a standard ground is unavailable or the soil is poorly conductive. It is typically elevated above the earth.
  • Functional Difference: Ground screens rely on contact with the earth; counterpoises act as a capacitive substitute for the earth.

Counterpoise Installation Requirements

To be effective, a counterpoise must be constructed according to the operating frequency to ensure resonance and efficiency.

  • Requires at least four radial wires.
  • Radials must be cut to the correct length (1/4 wavelength) for the operating frequency.
  • Wires should be spread out evenly (90 degrees apart) from the base of the antenna.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your team is tasked with establishing an HF radio site in a rocky, arid region where the soil conductivity is extremely poor. You must implement a counterpoise system for your vertical whip antenna to ensure reliable communications with the Battalion COC.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the operating frequency and calculate the 1/4 wavelength for the radial wires.
  2. Measure and cut four lengths of copper wire to the calculated length.
  3. Connect the four wires to the ground terminal of the antenna base or the radio's ground lug.
  4. Deploy the wires radially from the antenna, ensuring they are approximately 90 degrees apart.
  5. Secure the ends of the radials using ground stakes, ensuring they are taut and elevated if required by the specific antenna kit.
Conclusion

Summary: We have discussed how ground systems reduce loss and improve efficiency. We differentiated between buried ground screens and elevated counterpoises, and we covered the specific requirements for installing a four-radial counterpoise system.

Closing Statement: A radio operator who understands the ground is an operator who can communicate anywhere. Never neglect your ground system; it is the foundation of your signal's strength.

Lesson 34: Directional Antenna Orientation

TLO: TLO-034

Introduction

Gain Attention: A directional antenna is like a sniper rifle; it concentrates all its energy into a narrow beam to hit a specific target. However, if that rifle is misaligned by even a few degrees, you will miss the target entirely. In the world of radio, a misaligned directional antenna means your signal is being wasted on empty space while your intended receiver hears nothing but static.

Overview: This lesson focuses on the precise orientation of directional antennas, including the calculation of azimuths and the identification of radiation patterns to maximize signal gain.

Objectives:

  • Define the term 'azimuth' as it relates to antenna orientation per MCRP 3-40.3C.
  • Identify the major lobe of an antenna pattern per MCRP 3-40.3C.
  • Calculate the required azimuth for antenna orientation within +/- 3 degrees.
Body

Azimuth and Orientation Fundamentals

Azimuth is the horizontal angle measured clockwise from a north reference (typically grid north or magnetic north) to the direction of the distant station.

  • Proper orientation ensures the antenna's energy is concentrated toward the receiver.
  • Orientation is critical for directional antennas like the Yagi, Vee, or Sloping Wire.
  • Reference MCRP 3-40.3C Appendix A for standardized definitions.

Understanding Radiation Patterns

Every antenna has a radiation pattern that shows where the energy is strongest.

  • Major Lobe: The area of maximum radiation intensity where the most gain is achieved.
  • Minor Lobes/Side Lobes: Areas of unintended radiation that waste power and can increase the chance of detection by the enemy.
  • Nulls: Directions in which the antenna radiates little to no energy.

Calculating and Applying the Azimuth

To achieve maximum gain, the major lobe must be aligned precisely with the distant station's location.

  • Determine your location and the distant station's location using grid coordinates.
  • Calculate the grid-to-magnetic conversion (G-M angle) if using a lensatic compass.
  • The standard for alignment is within +/- 3 degrees to ensure the peak of the major lobe is utilized.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are located at Grid 12S VF 1234 5678. You need to establish a directional link with a station located at Grid 12S VF 2234 6678. Using a map and a directional antenna, you must calculate the bearing and orient the antenna's major lobe.

Practice Steps:

  1. Plot both stations on the map and draw a line between them.
  2. Use a protractor to determine the grid azimuth from your position to the distant station.
  3. Apply the G-M angle for your current location to convert the grid azimuth to a magnetic azimuth.
  4. Physically rotate the directional antenna so that its primary radiating element (the major lobe) is aligned with the calculated magnetic azimuth.
  5. Verify the alignment using a compass, ensuring the error is no more than +/- 3 degrees.
Conclusion

Summary: We defined azimuth, identified the importance of the major lobe in radiation patterns, and practiced the calculations necessary to align a directional antenna.

Closing Statement: Precision in orientation is the hallmark of a professional communicator. By mastering azimuth calculations and lobe alignment, you ensure that your signal reaches the target with maximum intensity.

Lesson 35: HF Antenna Selection and Propagation

TLO: TLO-035

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are operating in a deep valley in a mountainous region. Your standard whip antenna is failing to reach the Combat Operations Center (COC) only 50 miles away because the terrain is blocking your line-of-sight. Understanding HF propagation is the difference between a successful CASEVAC call and total radio silence. Today, we will learn how to 'bounce' signals off the atmosphere to overcome terrain and distance.

Overview: This lesson covers the fundamental principles of HF propagation including Groundwave, Skywave, and NVIS, and provides the criteria for selecting the optimal antenna based on mission requirements.

Objectives:

  • TLO-035: Determine the appropriate HF antenna type.
  • ELO-093: Describe the characteristics of Groundwave, Skywave, and NVIS propagation.
  • ELO-094: Compare the gain and take-off angle characteristics of each antenna.
Body

HF Propagation Fundamentals

Radio waves travel from the transmitter to the receiver in three primary ways depending on frequency and antenna type.

  • Groundwave: Follows the curvature of the earth; best for short distances (0-50 miles) using vertical polarization.
  • Skywave: Reflects off the ionosphere; used for long-range communication (100 to thousands of miles) but has a 'skip zone' where no signal is received.
  • Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS): Radiates at high angles (70-90 degrees) to reflect back down locally (0-300 miles), effectively 'filling in' the skip zone and overcoming terrain.

Antenna Characteristics and Take-off Angles

The 'Take-off Angle' is the angle above the horizon that an antenna radiates its energy. This determines the distance the signal will travel.

  • Vertical Whip: Low take-off angle; excellent for Groundwave but poor for NVIS.
  • Half-Wave Dipole: Variable take-off angle based on height above ground; highly versatile for medium to long-range Skywave.
  • AS-2259/GR: High take-off angle (near 90 degrees); specifically designed for NVIS and short-range communication in restrictive terrain.

Antenna Selection Criteria

To select the right antenna, the operator must evaluate the distance to the distant station, the frequency assigned, and the environmental obstacles.

  • Short Range (0-300 miles) with terrain: Select NVIS (AS-2259 or low Dipole).
  • Medium Range (300-1500 miles): Select Dipole or Inverted Vee at moderate heights.
  • Long Range (1500+ miles): Select low take-off angle antennas like the Sloping Vee or Vertical Half-Rhombic.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are the Radio Supervisor for a Reconnaissance team inserted 150 miles from the extraction point. You are located in a heavily forested ravine. You have been assigned a frequency of 5.0 MHz. You have an AS-2259 kit, a Dipole kit, and a 10ft Whip.

Practice Steps:

  1. Analyze the distance requirement (150 miles = NVIS/Short Range Skywave).
  2. Evaluate the terrain (Ravine = High take-off angle required).
  3. Compare available antennas based on MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 4.
  4. Select the AS-2259/GR as the primary antenna to ensure NVIS propagation.
  5. Justify the selection based on the 90-degree take-off angle required to clear the ravine walls.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the three types of HF propagation and how antenna take-off angles dictate the effective range of our communications. Selecting the right antenna is not a guess; it is a technical decision based on distance, frequency, and terrain.

Closing Statement: The ability to communicate is a weapon system. By mastering antenna selection, you ensure that the MAGTF commander maintains command and control, regardless of the distance or the height of the mountains between you and your objective.

Lesson 36: Installation of the AS-2259/GR Antenna

TLO: TLO-036

Introduction

Gain Attention: The AS-2259/GR is the most effective tool in the Marine Corps inventory for short-range HF communications in jungle or mountainous environments. However, if installed incorrectly, it becomes a 15-foot lightning rod or a source of RF burns for your team. Precision in installation is a matter of both mission success and physical safety.

Overview: This lesson provides the knowledge and skills to safely and effectively install the AS-2259/GR antenna kit for NVIS operations.

Objectives:

  • TLO-036: Perform the installation of an AS-2259/GR antenna.
  • ELO-095: Identify the components of the AS-2259/GR antenna kit.
  • ELO-096: Explain safety precautions for HF antenna installation.
  • ELO-097: Assemble the mast sections and radiating elements.
Body

Safety and Siting Considerations

Before unpacking the kit, the site must be surveyed for hazards according to MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 8.

  • Power Lines: Ensure the site is at least twice the height of the antenna away from any power lines.
  • RF Hazards: Establish a keep-out zone to prevent personnel from touching the radiating elements during transmission.
  • Grounding: The antenna must be properly grounded to the radio set to prevent equipment damage and electrical shock.

AS-2259/GR Component Identification

The AS-2259/GR is a specialized kit. Operators must ensure all components are present and serviceable.

  • Mast Sections: Seven fiberglass sections, including one top section and six interchangeable lower sections.
  • Top Assembly: Contains the matching transformer and connections for the radiating elements.
  • Radiating Elements: Four wire elements that also serve as the guy wires for the mast.
  • Base Stake and Ground Cable: Provides the physical foundation and electrical ground path.

Assembly and Erection Procedures

Follow a structured sequence to ensure the mast is stable and the elements are properly tensioned.

  • Drive the base stake into the ground and attach the base of the first mast section.
  • Assemble the mast sections on the ground, attaching the top assembly and radiating elements.
  • Carefully raise the mast vertically, ensuring it remains straight.
  • Secure the four radiating elements to the ground stakes at 90-degree intervals, providing tension to stabilize the mast.
  • Connect the coaxial cable to the radio and perform a VSWR check.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your unit has just arrived at a new Patrol Base. You are tasked with establishing an NVIS link back to the Battalion HQ. You have been provided an AS-2259/GR kit and must set it up within 15 minutes.

Practice Steps:

  1. Conduct a site survey to ensure clearance from power lines and overhead obstructions.
  2. Inventory the AS-2259/GR kit against the technical manual.
  3. Drive the base stake and assemble the seven mast sections.
  4. Attach the radiating elements to the top assembly.
  5. Raise the mast and secure the elements to the ground stakes, ensuring the mast is perfectly vertical.
  6. Connect the ground cable and the RF feed line to the radio set.
Conclusion

Summary: We have identified the components, safety requirements, and assembly steps for the AS-2259/GR. This antenna is essential for NVIS comms, but its effectiveness depends entirely on the quality of your installation.

Closing Statement: A radio is only as good as its antenna. By following these procedures, you ensure that your team has a stable, safe, and effective communication link when it matters most.

Lesson 37: Installation of the OE-254 Antenna

TLO: TLO-037

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are in a high-intensity conflict where your manpack whip antenna is failing to reach the Combat Operations Center (COC) due to terrain. According to MCRP 3-40.3C, the antenna is the one variable an operator has the most control over. By properly installing the OE-254, you can transform a marginal, static-filled net into a crystal-clear link that ensures your unit's calls for fire and medical evacuations are heard.

Overview: This lesson covers the identification of OE-254 components, tactical siting considerations to maximize signal propagation, and the step-by-step assembly and installation of the antenna system.

Objectives:

  • TLO-037: Perform the installation of an OE-254 antenna.
  • ELO-098: Identify the components of the OE-254 antenna kit.
  • ELO-099: Explain siting considerations for the OE-254 antenna.
  • ELO-100: Assemble the OE-254 mast and radiator assembly.
Body

OE-254 Component Identification

Before deployment, every operator must verify the serviceability of the OE-254 kit. Missing or damaged components will directly degrade VHF line-of-sight communications.

  • Mast Base and Mast Sections: The structural foundation of the antenna.
  • Guy Plates and Guy Ropes: Essential for maintaining a vertical, stable mast under wind load.
  • Radiator Elements: The active components that facilitate signal transmission and reception.
  • Base Stake and Grounding Equipment: Critical for safety and signal stability.

Tactical Siting and Signal Propagation

The effectiveness of a VHF antenna is heavily dependent on its physical location. Operators must analyze the terrain to avoid signal masking.

  • Ground Slope: Ensure the site is level enough to support a vertical mast without risking collapse.
  • Overhead Obstructions: Avoid power lines (safety hazard) and heavy foliage which absorbs VHF energy.
  • Distance to Radio: Keep the cable run within technical limits to minimize signal attenuation (line loss).

Assembly and Vertical Installation

Proper assembly ensures the antenna operates at the correct resonance and prevents physical damage to the equipment.

  • Locking Mast Sections: Each section must be fully seated and locked to prevent the mast from telescoping downward.
  • Radiator Seating: Elements must be securely attached to the feed cone to ensure electrical continuity.
  • Tensioning Guy Lines: Use a 'star' pattern to ensure the mast is perfectly vertical and tensioned equally.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your platoon has established a patrol base in a wooded valley. You are ordered to establish a VHF retransmission point on a nearby ridge to maintain comms with the Company HQ.

Practice Steps:

  1. Conduct a site survey of the ridge, identifying a level area clear of overhead power lines.
  2. Inventory the OE-254 kit, laying out all mast sections and radiator elements.
  3. Assemble the radiator assembly and attach the coaxial cable.
  4. Erect the mast sections one at a time, securing guy lines at the 15-foot and 30-foot levels.
  5. Perform a radio check to verify signal strength and verticality of the mast.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the identification of the OE-254 components, the critical nature of siting for VHF propagation, and the technical steps required for a stable, vertical installation.

Closing Statement: The OE-254 is a force multiplier. Your ability to install this system correctly ensures that the MAGTF remains a connected, lethal force regardless of the terrain.

Lesson 38: Antenna Farm Planning and Layout

TLO: TLO-038

Introduction

Gain Attention: In a modern Command Post, dozens of radios are transmitting simultaneously. Without a plan, these systems will interfere with each other, creating 'electronic fratricide' that can shut down our own communications more effectively than the enemy. Mastering the antenna farm layout is the difference between a functional COC and a useless pile of interference.

Overview: This lesson provides the framework for planning an antenna farm, focusing on the types of command post configurations, technical placement considerations, and the calculation of separation distances to prevent cosite interference.

Objectives:

  • TLO-038: Plan an antenna farm layout.
  • ELO-101: Describe the types of antenna farms.
  • ELO-102: Analyze technical considerations for antenna placement.
  • ELO-103: Determine minimum separation distances between antennas.
Body

Command Post Antenna Farm Configurations

The layout of an antenna farm is dictated by the echelon of command and the tactical mission.

  • Tactical CP: Small, mobile, and rapidly deployed; focuses on immediate maneuver nets.
  • Main CP: High density of systems (HF, VHF, UHF, SATCOM); requires complex interference management.
  • Rear CP: Focuses on sustainment and long-haul links, often utilizing more permanent antenna structures.

Technical Placement Considerations

Technical factors must be balanced against tactical security to ensure the farm remains operational and survivable.

  • Frequency Separation: Grouping similar frequency bands while maintaining distance between high-power transmitters and sensitive receivers.
  • Polarization: Ensuring all antennas in a net use the same polarization (vertical vs. horizontal) to avoid 20dB+ signal loss.
  • Power Line Interference: Siting antennas away from civilian power grids to reduce man-made noise floors.

Separation Distances and Cosite Interference

Cosite interference occurs when a transmitter's signal overwhelms a nearby receiver. This is mitigated through physical distance and frequency management.

  • Horizontal Separation: The primary method for reducing interference between antennas in the same frequency band.
  • Vertical Separation: Utilizing different mast heights to create isolation between antennas.
  • Power Output Analysis: High-power HF transmitters require significantly more 'buffer' space than low-power VHF handhelds.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are the Comm Chief for a Battalion Main CP. You are given a list of 12 radio nets (4 HF, 6 VHF, 2 UHF) and a 100m x 100m plot of land. You must design the layout.

Practice Steps:

  1. Group radios by frequency band (HF, VHF, UHF).
  2. Identify the highest power transmitters and place them on the perimeter.
  3. Calculate minimum separation distances based on MCRP 6-22D Chapter 8 standards.
  4. Draft a site map showing the location, polarization, and frequency of every antenna.
  5. Brief the layout, justifying the placement based on terrain and interference mitigation.
Conclusion

Summary: We have analyzed the different types of antenna farms, the technical requirements for polarization and frequency management, and the necessity of maintaining strict separation distances.

Closing Statement: A well-planned antenna farm is invisible when it works, but a failure in planning is felt by every Marine on the net. Plan with precision to ensure the Commander's intent is always communicable.

Lesson 39: Construction of the Half-Wave Dipole Antenna

TLO: TLO-039

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are operating in a deep valley where your standard vehicle whip antenna cannot clear the terrain. Your mission depends on establishing a reliable HF link back to the COC. By the end of this period of instruction, you will know how to turn a spool of copper wire and a few insulators into a high-performance half-wave dipole that can punch through atmospheric noise and terrain obstacles.

Overview: This lesson covers the mathematical calculation, physical configuration, and construction techniques required to build a center-fed half-wave dipole antenna using field-expedient materials and MCRP 3-40.3C standards.

Objectives:

  • TLO-039: Given a frequency, wire, insulators, a transmission line, and MCRP 6-22D, construct a half-wave dipole antenna.
  • ELO-104: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole antenna.
  • ELO-105: Describe the configuration of a center-fed doublet.
  • ELO-106: Measure and cut antenna wire elements.
Body

Calculating Antenna Length

To ensure resonance at the desired operating frequency, the antenna must be cut to a specific length. The standard formula for a half-wave dipole in feet is 468 divided by the frequency in Megahertz (MHz).

  • Formula: L (feet) = 468 / Frequency (MHz)
  • This result provides the total length of the antenna from end to end.
  • Accuracy must be within 1% to ensure a low Standing Wave Ratio (SWR).

Center-Fed Doublet Configuration

A half-wave dipole, also known as a center-fed doublet, consists of two distinct elements. Each element is a quarter-wavelength long.

  • The transmission line (coax or twin-lead) connects at the center insulator.
  • Two wire elements extend in opposite directions from the center.
  • Insulators are used at the center and both ends to isolate the antenna from the support structures.

Measuring and Cutting Techniques

Precision in measurement is critical. When cutting wire, the operator must account for the 'pigtails' needed to secure the wire to the insulators.

  • Measure the total calculated length first.
  • Divide the total length by two to determine the length of each quarter-wave element.
  • Add 6-12 inches of 'service loop' or excess wire to each end for wrapping around insulators and soldering/connecting to the transmission line.
Practical Application

Scenario: The platoon is assigned a primary HF frequency of 8.45 MHz. You are tasked with constructing a horizontal half-wave dipole to support long-haul communications.

Practice Steps:

  1. Calculate the total length: 468 / 8.45 = 55.38 feet.
  2. Divide by 2 for each element: 27.69 feet per side.
  3. Measure two lengths of WD-1/TT or copper wire to 28.5 feet (including excess for ties).
  4. Attach the two elements to a center insulator and connect the transmission line.
  5. Secure the far ends to insulators and prepare for hoisting.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the calculation of antenna length using the 468 formula, the physical layout of the center-fed doublet, and the practical steps to measure and cut the wire elements.

Closing Statement: The ability to fabricate an antenna from raw wire is a hallmark of a proficient communicator. This skill ensures that even if your primary equipment is damaged, the MAGTF maintains its ability to command and control.

Lesson 40: Antenna Length Theory and Calculation

TLO: TLO-040

Introduction

Gain Attention: Radio waves travel at the speed of light—300 million meters per second. However, because electricity travels slightly slower in wire than in free space, our antennas must be mathematically 'tuned' to match the wave. If your math is wrong, your signal stays in the radio as heat instead of going into the atmosphere as a wave.

Overview: This lesson focuses on the theoretical relationship between frequency and wavelength and the precise calculations required to determine antenna element lengths for HF operations.

Objectives:

  • TLO-040: Calculate the physical length of antenna elements.
  • ELO-107: Identify the constant values used in the antenna length formula.
  • ELO-108: Explain the inverse relationship between frequency and wavelength.
  • ELO-109: Calculate the length of a half-wave dipole antenna in feet.
Body

Frequency and Wavelength Relationship

There is an inverse relationship between frequency and wavelength. As the frequency of a signal increases, the physical length of the wave decreases.

  • Higher Frequency = Shorter Antenna.
  • Lower Frequency = Longer Antenna.
  • Understanding this prevents common errors when switching between day and night frequencies.

Standard Constants for Calculation

MCRP 3-40.3C provides specific constants to simplify the calculation of half-wave and quarter-wave antennas.

  • For length in feet: Use the constant 468 for a half-wave antenna.
  • For length in meters: Use the constant 143 for a half-wave antenna.
  • These constants account for the 'velocity factor' of electricity traveling through wire.

Mathematical Precision

Calculations must be accurate to two decimal places to remain within the 1% tolerance required for tactical radios.

  • Step 1: Identify the assigned frequency in MHz.
  • Step 2: Divide the constant (468) by the frequency.
  • Step 3: Round to the nearest hundredth.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are provided with three frequencies for a 24-hour period: 4.25 MHz, 12.10 MHz, and 22.50 MHz. You must calculate the exact half-wave dipole length for each to prepare the wire kits.

Practice Steps:

  1. Calculate for 4.25 MHz: 468 / 4.25 = 110.12 feet.
  2. Calculate for 12.10 MHz: 468 / 12.10 = 38.68 feet.
  3. Calculate for 22.50 MHz: 468 / 22.50 = 20.80 feet.
  4. Verify that as the frequency increased, the calculated length decreased.
Conclusion

Summary: You have learned the inverse relationship between frequency and wavelength, the constants 468 and 143, and the method for precise length calculation.

Closing Statement: Precision in your calculations is the difference between a clear voice link and a radio that overheats and fails. Master the math, and you master the spectrum.

Lesson 41: Installation of the AS-2259/GR NVIS Antenna

TLO: TLO-041

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are operating in a deep valley, only 50 miles from your higher headquarters. Your standard whip antenna is failing because the signal is being absorbed by the surrounding terrain. This is the 'skip zone'—where tactical communications go to die. The AS-2259/GR is your solution to bridge that gap using Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS), allowing you to communicate over obstacles by bouncing your signal off the ionosphere at a steep angle.

Overview: This lesson covers the fundamental principles of NVIS propagation, the identification of AS-2259/GR components, and the step-by-step procedures for assembling and erecting the antenna system to support short-range HF communications.

Objectives:

  • TLO-041: Demonstrate the installation of an AS-2259/GR antenna.
  • ELO-110: Identify the components of the AS-2259/GR antenna kit.
  • ELO-111: Describe the characteristics of Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation.
  • ELO-112: Assemble the AS-2259/GR mast and radiating elements.
Body

NVIS Propagation Characteristics

Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) is a technique used to provide reliable communications in the 0-300 mile range, effectively eliminating the skip zone common in HF communications.

  • Requires high take-off angles (60-90 degrees) to ensure the signal reflects back to Earth locally.
  • Operates typically in the 2-12 MHz frequency range depending on atmospheric conditions.
  • Ideal for mountainous terrain or heavily vegetated areas where line-of-sight is impossible.

AS-2259/GR Component Identification

The AS-2259/GR is a tactical HF antenna designed specifically for NVIS. Operators must be able to identify all kit components to ensure rapid deployment.

  • Mast Sections: Seven interlocking sections that provide the vertical structure.
  • Top Truck: The assembly at the top of the mast that houses the matching transformer.
  • Radiating Elements: Two crossed-dipole wire assemblies that also serve as guy wires.
  • Base Plate and Stakes: Provides the foundation and anchoring for the system.

Assembly and Installation Procedures

Proper assembly ensures both electrical performance and structural integrity. All connections must be hand-tight to prevent damage while maintaining conductivity.

  • Site Selection: Choose a level area approximately 60x60 feet.
  • Mast Assembly: Connect mast sections sequentially while attaching the radiating elements to the top truck.
  • Erection: Carefully raise the mast while tensioning the radiating elements/guy wires.
  • Connection: Attach the RF cable to the base and ensure the system is grounded.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your unit is established in a patrol base located in a canyon. You are tasked with establishing a command net with the Combat Operations Center (COC) located 45 miles away. You must deploy the AS-2259/GR to overcome the terrain masking.

Practice Steps:

  1. Inventory the AS-2259/GR kit using the technical manual.
  2. Select a suitable site and layout the base plate and stakes.
  3. Assemble the mast sections and attach the top truck.
  4. Deploy the radiating elements at 90-degree angles from each other.
  5. Erect the antenna and secure the guy wires to the stakes.
  6. Perform a radio check to verify signal strength and NVIS propagation.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the mechanics of NVIS propagation, identified the critical components of the AS-2259/GR, and practiced the assembly of the antenna. These skills allow for reliable HF communications in environments where standard antennas fail.

Closing Statement: Mastering the AS-2259/GR ensures that no matter the terrain, the Marine Corps maintains the ability to command and control the battlespace.

Lesson 42: Installation of the OE-254 VHF Antenna

TLO: TLO-042

Introduction

Gain Attention: In the world of VHF communications, height is king. Without a clear line-of-sight, your mission-critical data and voice traffic won't reach the receiver. The OE-254 Omni-Directional Antenna is the workhorse that extends your reach and ensures your signal clears the trees and terrain that would otherwise block your path.

Overview: This lesson focuses on the siting considerations for line-of-sight (LOS) communications, the identification of OE-254 components, and the physical assembly and erection of the antenna system.

Objectives:

  • TLO-042: Demonstrate the installation of an OE-254 antenna.
  • ELO-113: Identify the components of the OE-254 antenna kit.
  • ELO-114: Explain the siting considerations for a line-of-sight (LOS) antenna.
  • ELO-115: Perform the assembly of the OE-254 bicone antenna head.
Body

Siting and LOS Propagation

VHF signals travel primarily via line-of-sight. Understanding how terrain and placement affect this signal is critical for the radio operator.

  • Terrain Masking: Hills and buildings can completely block VHF signals.
  • Vegetation: Heavy foliage absorbs high-frequency energy, reducing range.
  • Antenna Height: Increasing the height of the antenna directly increases the radio horizon and signal clarity.

OE-254 Component Identification

The OE-254 is a rugged, bicone antenna. Familiarity with its components is essential for assembly under low-light or high-stress conditions.

  • Feedcone: The central hub where the elements attach and the signal is fed.
  • Antenna Elements: The screw-in rods that form the bicone shape.
  • Mast Sections: Lightweight aluminum tubes used to elevate the antenna.
  • Guy Ropes and Stakes: Essential for stabilizing the antenna at its full 30-foot height.

Assembly of the Bicone Head

The bicone head is the heart of the antenna. It must be assembled correctly to ensure the antenna is resonant across the 30-88 MHz VHF band.

  • Ensure all elements are fully seated into the feedcone to prevent signal loss.
  • Check the frequency configuration; the OE-254 is broadband and does not require tuning, but physical integrity is paramount.
  • Attach the coaxial cable to the feedcone before elevating the mast.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your platoon is tasked with providing a retransmission site on a designated hilltop. You must site and erect the OE-254 to ensure the company net maintains connectivity across the valley floor.

Practice Steps:

  1. Analyze the terrain to identify the highest point with the clearest line-of-sight.
  2. Unpack the OE-254 kit and verify all components are present.
  3. Assemble the bicone antenna head by securely threading all elements into the feedcone.
  4. Connect the RF cable to the feedcone and secure it to the mast.
  5. Assemble the mast sections and raise the antenna using the guy ropes for stability.
  6. Secure the guy ropes to stakes at the proper distance to ensure the mast is vertical and stable.
Conclusion

Summary: We have discussed the importance of siting for LOS communications, identified the OE-254 components, and demonstrated the assembly of the bicone head and mast.

Closing Statement: The OE-254 is a force multiplier. By properly siting and erecting this antenna, you ensure that the commander's intent is heard clearly across the entire AO.

Lesson 43: Construction of Field-Expedient Wire Antennas

TLO: TLO-043

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are operating in a dense jungle or a deep urban canyon where your standard whip antenna cannot reach the distant station. Your mission depends on getting a SITREP out, but your primary antenna is broken or insufficient. By the end of this lesson, you will possess the 'black magic' of radio communications: the ability to turn a spool of field wire and some basic math into a high-performance antenna system that can reach across the battlespace.

Overview: This lesson covers the technical requirements for calculating, assembling, and employing field-expedient wire antennas using WD-1/TT field wire and improvised insulators.

Objectives:

  • TLO-043: Construct a field-expedient wire antenna.
  • ELO-116: Calculate the physical length of a wire antenna.
  • ELO-117: Assemble antenna components including the radiator, insulators, and feed line connections.
Body

Antenna Length Calculation

To achieve resonance, an antenna must be cut to a specific length relative to its operating frequency. Per MCRP 3-40.3C Section III, the standard formula for a half-wave dipole is used to ensure the antenna efficiently radiates energy.

  • Formula: 468 divided by the frequency in MHz equals the total length in feet.
  • For a half-wave dipole, this total length is then divided by two to create two equal elements (legs).
  • Accuracy is critical; even a few inches of error can result in high VSWR and potential damage to the radio set.

Assembly and Component Integration

Construction requires the integration of the radiator (wire), insulators, and the feed line. Following MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 6, Marines must ensure mechanical strength and electrical conductivity.

  • Use WD-1/TT field wire as the primary radiating element.
  • Insulators (improvised from plastic, glass, or dry wood) must be used at the ends and center to prevent the signal from grounding out.
  • Utilize the clove hitch or square knot to secure wire to insulators to prevent slipping under tension.
  • Electrical connections must be stripped of insulation and twisted tightly to ensure metal-to-metal contact.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your team is established in a patrol base. You are assigned a frequency of 14.250 MHz and must establish a long-range HF link using a Half-Wave Dipole configuration. You have a spool of WD-1/TT, two plastic MRE spoons to use as insulators, and a multi-tool.

Practice Steps:

  1. Calculate the total antenna length (468 / 14.250).
  2. Measure and cut two equal lengths of WD-1/TT wire.
  3. Attach the wire ends to the improvised insulators using clove hitches.
  4. Strip 2 inches of insulation from the center ends and connect them to the coaxial feed line or radio adapter.
  5. Hoist the antenna into the air using para-cord, ensuring it is clear of metal obstructions.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the mathematical requirements for antenna resonance and the physical assembly techniques required by MCRP 3-40.3C. Remember: 468/Freq is your baseline for success.

Closing Statement: A Marine's ability to innovate with available materials is a force multiplier. Don't let a broken whip antenna be the reason your unit loses comms.

Lesson 44: Antenna Troubleshooting and Field Repair

TLO: TLO-044

Introduction

Gain Attention: The most sophisticated radio in the world is nothing more than an expensive paperweight if the antenna system is compromised. In the field, antennas are snagged by trees, snapped by vehicles, or degraded by corrosion. Your ability to quickly identify the fault and apply a 'combat fix' is what keeps the command and control loop closed.

Overview: This lesson focuses on identifying common antenna faults and performing the Western Union splice to restore electrical and structural integrity to wire antennas.

Objectives:

  • TLO-044: Troubleshoot a damaged antenna system to restore functionality.
  • ELO-118: Identify common antenna system faults.
  • ELO-119: Perform a Western Union splice on broken antenna wire.
Body

Identifying Antenna System Faults

Troubleshooting begins with a visual inspection and an understanding of how electrical faults manifest in radio performance. Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 6, operators must look for three primary issues.

  • Shorts: Occur when the radiating element touches the ground or a metal structure, causing energy to bleed off.
  • Opens: A break in the wire or a loose connection that prevents the signal from reaching the antenna.
  • High VSWR (Voltage Standing Wave Ratio): Indicated by the radio's internal meter; usually caused by incorrect length or poor grounding.

The Western Union Splice

When a wire antenna is severed, a simple knot is insufficient because it lacks electrical continuity. The Western Union splice is the military standard for repairing field wire (MCRP 3-40.3C, Page 6-2).

  • Strip approximately 4-6 inches of insulation from both broken ends.
  • Twist the wires together tightly, ensuring at least five wraps on each side of the center.
  • The splice must be mechanically strong enough to withstand the tension of being hoisted.
  • Seal the connection with electrical or friction tape to prevent moisture from corroding the copper/steel strands.
Practical Application

Scenario: During a night move, a vehicle drove over your inverted-vee antenna's leg, snapping the WD-1/TT wire. Your radio is showing a 'Check Antenna' fault. You must restore the link immediately using your field repair kit.

Practice Steps:

  1. Locate the break in the wire through visual and tactile inspection.
  2. Strip the insulation from both ends of the break using a multi-tool.
  3. Perform a Western Union splice, ensuring the wraps are tight and the connection is rigid.
  4. Apply electrical tape to the splice, overlapping the insulation on both sides.
  5. Re-tension the antenna and perform a radio check to verify the fault is cleared.
Conclusion

Summary: We have identified the symptoms of shorts and opens and mastered the Western Union splice. These skills ensure that antenna damage is only a temporary setback, not a mission failure.

Closing Statement: In the fleet, you won't always have a fresh antenna in the warehouse. Master these repairs now so you can keep the net alive when it matters most.

Lesson 45: Fabrication of Field-Expedient Ground Connections

TLO: TLO-045

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are in a hide site, your radio is functioning perfectly, and your antenna is cut to the exact frequency, yet your signal is barely breaking the squelch of the receiving station. In many tactical environments, the difference between a failed mission and successful communication is the quality of your ground. Without a low-resistance path to the earth, your radio energy has nowhere to go, effectively turning your equipment into an expensive paperweight.

Overview: This lesson covers the technical requirements for establishing a field-expedient ground, the environmental considerations for site selection, and the physical preparation of materials to ensure maximum conductivity.

Objectives:

  • TLO-045: Demonstrate the fabrication of a field-expedient ground connection.
  • ELO-120: Explain the requirements for a field-expedient ground.
  • ELO-121: Prepare the contact surfaces for a ground connection.
Body

Grounding Requirements and Environmental Safety

According to MCRP 3-40.3C, Section II, a ground must provide a low-resistance path to the earth to support efficient radio wave radiation.

  • Resistance: The goal is the lowest resistance possible; high resistance leads to power loss and potential equipment damage.
  • Moisture: Conductivity is directly related to soil moisture. In dry conditions, grounding effectiveness decreases significantly.
  • Environmental Safety: Ground rods must never be installed near drinking water supplies to prevent contamination of the water table.

Surface Preparation and Oxidation Prevention

Electrical conductivity is only as good as the point of contact. Metal-to-metal contact is mandatory for a low-resistance bond.

  • Cleaning: Use sandpaper or a scraper to remove all paint, rust, and oxidation from the ground rod and the wire.
  • Bare Metal: Surfaces must be polished to bare metal to ensure maximum surface area contact.
  • Protection: Once the connection is made using a clamp or wire wrap, it should be taped to prevent moisture from causing rapid oxidation.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your unit has established a temporary patrol base in a wooded area. You are tasked with setting up a manpack radio for long-range HF communication. You have a length of copper wire and a galvanized steel pipe to use as a ground.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify a location for the ground rod that is away from known water sources.
  2. Drive the pipe into the ground, seeking moist soil if available.
  3. Use a scraper or sandpaper to clean a 2-inch section of the pipe until bare metal is visible.
  4. Clean the end of the ground wire to remove any insulation or corrosion.
  5. Secure the wire to the cleaned section of the pipe using a ground clamp or tight wire wrap.
  6. Seal the connection with electrical tape to prevent oxidation.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the necessity of low-resistance grounds, the impact of soil moisture, and the critical requirement to protect water supplies. We also demonstrated the proper method for cleaning contact surfaces to ensure a solid electrical bond.

Closing Statement: A radio operator who ignores the ground is an operator who ignores their primary weapon system. Master these field-expedient techniques to ensure your message gets through, regardless of the terrain.

Lesson 46: Installation of Antenna Counterpoise Systems

TLO: TLO-046

Introduction

Gain Attention: What do you do when the ground is too rocky to drive a rod, or you are operating in a desert where the sand is so dry it acts as an insulator? In these environments, a traditional ground is impossible. To maintain communications, you must create an artificial ground—a counterpoise—to complete your radio circuit.

Overview: This lesson defines the counterpoise, explains its role in high-resistance soil environments, and details the physical installation requirements per MCRP 3-40.3C.

Objectives:

  • TLO-046: Perform the installation of an antenna counterpoise.
  • ELO-122: Define the term 'counterpoise' and its purpose in a radio circuit.
  • ELO-123: Describe the physical requirements for a counterpoise installation.
Body

The Counterpoise Concept

A counterpoise is a substitute for a ground connection used when the earth's resistance is too high for a standard ground rod to be effective.

  • Purpose: It acts as the 'other half' of the antenna system, providing a return path for RF current.
  • Application: Essential in desert, rocky terrain, or when operating from the upper floors of buildings.

Physical Installation Standards

MCRP 3-40.3C specifies strict physical parameters to ensure the counterpoise functions correctly without losing energy to the earth.

  • Insulation: Unlike a ground rod, a counterpoise must be insulated from the ground. It should be suspended above the earth or laid on insulators.
  • Sizing: The counterpoise must be at least equal to, or larger than, the physical size of the antenna it is supporting.
  • Connection: The counterpoise wire must be connected directly to the radio's ground terminal or the antenna's matching network ground.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are operating in a rocky plateau where the soil depth is less than 3 inches. You are deploying a vertical whip antenna and must install a counterpoise to ensure the radio can tune the frequency.

Practice Steps:

  1. Measure the length of your primary antenna radiator.
  2. Cut a counterpoise wire that is at least the same length as the antenna (preferably slightly longer).
  3. Connect one end of the counterpoise wire to the ground terminal of the radio or antenna base.
  4. Lay the wire out away from the radio, ensuring it is supported by insulators (like dry wood or plastic) to keep it from making direct contact with the high-resistance soil.
  5. Ensure the wire is clear of foot traffic to prevent trip hazards and signal interference.
Conclusion

Summary: A counterpoise is your primary alternative when the earth refuses to provide a natural ground. By ensuring it is properly sized and insulated, you can maintain a high-performance radio circuit in the most difficult geographical conditions.

Closing Statement: Adaptability is a hallmark of Marine Corps communications. When the ground fails you, the counterpoise ensures the mission continues.

Lesson 47: Antenna Polarization Requirements

TLO: TLO-047

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are in a high-stakes tactical environment. You have the correct frequency, your radio is powered on, and you are within range, but your transmission is barely audible through a wall of static. You check your connections, but everything looks solid. The culprit? Your antenna is oriented horizontally while the receiving station is vertical. In the world of radio communications, being 'off' by 90 degrees can mean the difference between a clear command and a total communications failure.

Overview: This lesson covers the fundamental principles of antenna polarization, the distinction between vertical and horizontal orientations, and how to select the correct polarization based on the transmission type and tactical environment.

Objectives:

  • TLO-047: Apply antenna polarization requirements.
  • ELO-124: Define vertical and horizontal polarization.
  • ELO-125: Explain the advantages of vertical versus horizontal polarization for different transmission types.
Body

Defining Polarization

Polarization is determined by the orientation of the electric field (E-plane) of the electromagnetic wave relative to the earth's surface. If the E-plane is perpendicular to the earth, it is vertically polarized. If it is parallel, it is horizontally polarized.

  • The physical position of the antenna radiator determines the polarization.
  • Vertical antennas (like whips) produce vertical polarization.
  • Horizontal antennas (like dipoles suspended between trees) produce horizontal polarization.

Tactical Application of Polarization

The choice of polarization significantly impacts signal propagation and noise reception. Per MCRP 3-40.3C, specific transmission types favor specific orientations.

  • Vertical Polarization: Preferred for ground wave transmission as it follows the earth's curvature more effectively and is standard for mobile/whip antennas.
  • Horizontal Polarization: Often used for sky wave (HF) to reduce the pickup of man-made noise, which is predominantly vertically polarized.
  • Cross-Polarization: When the transmitting and receiving antennas have different polarizations, a significant signal loss (up to 20dB or more) occurs.
Practical Application

Scenario: A Marine radio team is tasked with establishing a long-range HF sky wave link back to the COC while operating in an urban environment with high man-made electrical noise. They have a wire antenna kit and two masts.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the transmission type (Sky wave).
  2. Determine the noise environment (High man-made noise).
  3. Select the appropriate polarization (Horizontal) to minimize noise and optimize the sky wave path.
  4. Orient the wire antenna parallel to the ground to achieve horizontal polarization.
Conclusion

Summary: We have defined polarization as the orientation of the E-plane and discussed why vertical is used for ground waves while horizontal is often preferred for sky waves to mitigate noise.

Closing Statement: Understanding polarization ensures that your signal reaches its destination with maximum strength. Do not let a 90-degree mistake compromise your mission.

Lesson 48: Calculating Antenna Length

TLO: TLO-048

Introduction

Gain Attention: In a survival or tactical scenario, your issued antenna might break or be lost. As a communicator, you must be able to fabricate an antenna from a spool of WD-1/TT field wire. However, if you cut that wire to a random length, your radio's energy will reflect back into the transmitter, potentially frying the internal components and ensuring your message is never heard. Precision in length is precision in lethality.

Overview: This lesson provides the mathematical formulas and procedures required to calculate the physical length of half-wave and quarter-wave antennas to ensure resonance at a specific frequency.

Objectives:

  • TLO-048: Calculate the physical length of the antenna wire.
  • ELO-126: Identify the standard formula for calculating a half-wave dipole antenna.
  • ELO-127: Calculate the physical length of a quarter-wave vertical antenna.
Body

The Half-Wave Dipole Formula

To achieve resonance, an antenna must be cut to a specific fraction of the wavelength. For a half-wave dipole, the standard formula accounts for the velocity factor of wire.

  • Formula: Length (in feet) = 468 / Frequency (in MHz).
  • This formula provides the total length of the dipole from end to end.
  • Example: For 10 MHz, the length is 46.8 feet.

The Quarter-Wave Vertical Formula

A quarter-wave antenna (often used for whips or ground-plane antennas) is half the length of a dipole for the same frequency.

  • Formula: Length (in feet) = 234 / Frequency (in MHz).
  • This represents the length of the vertical radiator element.
  • Accuracy is critical; calculations should be within a 1% margin of error to maintain a low Standing Wave Ratio (SWR).
Practical Application

Scenario: You are assigned a frequency of 14.250 MHz. You need to construct a field-expedient half-wave dipole and a quarter-wave vertical antenna using field wire.

Practice Steps:

  1. Apply the half-wave formula: 468 / 14.250 = 32.84 feet.
  2. Apply the quarter-wave formula: 234 / 14.250 = 16.42 feet.
  3. Measure the wire using a tape measure, ensuring no kinks or loops.
  4. Cut the wire and prepare the center insulator for the dipole or the base mount for the vertical.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the critical formulas for antenna construction: 468/f for half-wave and 234/f for quarter-wave antennas.

Closing Statement: The ability to calculate and cut an antenna to the exact frequency is a hallmark of a professional communicator. Master these numbers, and you will never be without a way to reach the net.

Lesson 49: Antenna Orientation and Radiation Patterns

TLO: TLO-049

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are in a high-stakes tactical environment, and your life depends on a single transmission. You key the handset, but the distant station hears nothing but static. You have the right frequency and the right power, but your antenna is pointed 30 degrees off-target. In the world of radio communications, 'close enough' is a failure. Proper antenna orientation is the difference between a clear command and a lost connection.

Overview: This lesson covers the fundamental concepts of antenna radiation patterns, the difference between omnidirectional and directional antennas, and the technical process of calculating and applying an azimuth to ensure maximum signal-to-noise ratio.

Objectives:

  • Identify the radiation patterns for omnidirectional and directional antennas (ELO-128).
  • Calculate the azimuth for antenna orientation (ELO-129).
  • Demonstrate antenna orientation for maximum signal strength (TLO-049).
Body

Radiation Patterns and Directionality

Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 2, Section I, radiation patterns represent the energy distribution of an antenna in space. Understanding these patterns allows an operator to predict where the signal will be strongest.

  • Omnidirectional Antennas: Radiate energy equally in all directions (360 degrees) on the horizontal plane, typically used for mobile operations or net control stations.
  • Directional Antennas: Concentrate energy in a specific direction, providing 'gain' toward the distant station while reducing interference from other directions.
  • Nulls and Lobes: Lobes are areas of high signal strength; nulls are areas of little to no signal. Operators must align the main lobe with the distant station.

Azimuth Calculation and Orientation

To achieve maximum signal transfer, the antenna must be physically aligned with the distant station's location using a calculated azimuth.

  • Determining Grid Azimuth: Use the grid coordinates of the local and distant stations to determine the line of bearing.
  • Magnetic Conversion: Apply the G-M angle to convert the grid azimuth to a magnetic azimuth for use with a lensatic compass.
  • Physical Alignment: Align the antenna's boom or main radiating element perpendicular to or in line with the azimuth, depending on the specific antenna type (e.g., Dipole vs. Yagi).
Practical Application

Scenario: You are the RTO for a reconnaissance team. You are tasked with establishing a point-to-point HF link with the Combat Operations Center (COC) located 50 miles away at Grid 12S VF 1234 5678. You are currently at Grid 12S VF 9876 5432.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the appropriate antenna type (Directional) for the distance and mission.
  2. Calculate the grid azimuth from your position to the COC.
  3. Convert the grid azimuth to a magnetic azimuth using the local G-M angle.
  4. Use a lensatic compass to identify the line of bearing.
  5. Physically orient the antenna system so the main radiation lobe is aligned within +/- 3 degrees of the calculated azimuth.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the identification of radiation patterns and the precise calculation of azimuths. By mastering these skills, you ensure that the energy produced by your radio is focused where it is needed most.

Closing Statement: Precision in orientation is a hallmark of a professional communicator. Do not let a lack of attention to detail be the reason your message fails to get through.

Lesson 50: Antenna Grounding and Counterpoise Systems

TLO: TLO-050

Introduction

Gain Attention: Many operators believe the antenna is just the wire or the whip they see above ground. In reality, for many tactical antennas, the ground beneath your feet is the 'other half' of the antenna system. If you have a poor ground, you have a broken antenna. Without proper grounding, your radio's efficiency can drop by over 50%, wasting battery life and killing your range.

Overview: This lesson explains the theory of grounded antennas, the impact of soil conductivity, and the practical steps for installing grounding stakes and counterpoise systems to maximize radiation efficiency.

Objectives:

  • Describe the theory of grounded antennas and the impact of Earth conductivity (ELO-130).
  • Install a counterpoise system for a tactical antenna (ELO-131).
  • Perform the installation of an antenna grounding system (TLO-050).
Body

Grounded Antenna Theory

Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 2, Section II, the Earth acts as a reflecting surface for radio waves. A grounded antenna uses the Earth to create a 'mirror image' of the radiating element.

  • Circuit Completion: The ground system provides a low-resistance path to complete the RF circuit.
  • Earth Conductivity: Moist, loamy soil provides excellent conductivity, while dry, sandy, or rocky soil provides poor conductivity, requiring artificial ground enhancements.
  • Safety: Proper grounding also protects equipment and personnel from lightning strikes and static buildup.

Grounding Methods and Counterpoises

When the natural Earth conductivity is insufficient, operators must use artificial means to improve the ground connection.

  • Ground Stakes: Driven into the Earth to reach moist soil; multiple stakes can be connected in parallel to reduce resistance.
  • Counterpoise: A network of wires (radials) balanced above the ground. It is used when a true Earth ground is impossible to achieve (e.g., on top of a building or in extremely rocky soil).
  • Installation: Radials should be spread out like spokes on a wheel, extending from the base of the antenna.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are setting up an HF antenna in a desert environment where the soil is extremely dry and sandy. The radio is struggling to tune, and signal reports are weak. You must install a counterpoise system to establish a reliable circuit.

Practice Steps:

  1. Inspect the antenna base and identify the grounding terminal.
  2. Unroll the counterpoise radial wires from the kit.
  3. Lay out the radials in a symmetrical pattern around the antenna base, ensuring they are fully extended.
  4. Secure the radials to the ground using stakes or weights to prevent movement.
  5. Connect the central hub of the counterpoise to the radio's ground terminal using the shortest possible lead to minimize resistance.
Conclusion

Summary: We have discussed how the Earth completes the antenna circuit and how to compensate for poor soil using counterpoise systems. A well-grounded antenna is an efficient antenna.

Closing Statement: Never settle for a marginal ground. Taking the extra ten minutes to properly install your grounding system can be the difference between mission success and total communication blackout.

Lesson 51: Frequency Band Analysis and Propagation Modes

TLO: TLO-051

Introduction
