Gain Attention: Imagine you are a Radio Operator in a mountainous region. Your unit is 50 miles away, separated by a massive ridgeline. You try to key the handset on your VHF radio, but all you get is static. Understanding the electromagnetic spectrum isn't just for scientists—it's the difference between a successful CASEVAC call and total radio silence. Today, we learn how to choose the right frequency to 'punch through' the terrain.

Overview: This lesson covers the characteristics of the HF, VHF, and UHF frequency bands and the two primary modes of radio wave propagation: Ground Wave and Sky Wave.

Objectives:

  • ELO-132: State the frequency ranges and characteristics for the HF, VHF, and UHF bands.
  • ELO-133: Differentiate between Ground Wave and Sky Wave propagation modes.
  • ELO-134: Select the optimal frequency band for a specific communication path.
Body

The Military Radio Frequency Spectrum

Per MCRP 3-40.3C Figure 1-1, tactical radios operate within three primary bands, each with distinct boundaries and behaviors.

  • High Frequency (HF): 3 MHz to 30 MHz. Capable of long-range communication via sky wave.
  • Very High Frequency (VHF): 30 MHz to 300 MHz. Standard for FM tactical communications; primarily Line of Sight (LOS).
  • Ultra High Frequency (UHF): 300 MHz to 3 GHz. Used for LOS, ground-to-air, and satellite communications (SATCOM).

Propagation Fundamentals

Radio waves travel from the transmitter to the receiver in two primary ways depending on frequency and antenna type.

  • Ground Wave: Follows the curvature of the Earth. Best at lower frequencies; affected by terrain and soil conductivity.
  • Sky Wave: Radiates upward to the ionosphere and is reflected back to Earth. Enables 'over-the-horizon' communication.
  • Skip Zone: The area between the end of the ground wave and the point where the first sky wave returns to Earth where no signal is received.

Frequency Selection Criteria

Selecting the correct band requires balancing distance, terrain, and atmospheric conditions per MCRP 3-40.3C Table 1-1.

  • Short range (0-30 miles): VHF/UHF Ground Wave is typically preferred.
  • Medium to Long range (30-1500+ miles): HF Sky Wave is required.
  • Obstructions: If a mountain blocks LOS, HF Sky Wave or NVIS must be utilized regardless of short distance.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are assigned to a reconnaissance team 85 miles from the Combat Operations Center (COC). You have a PRC-150 (HF) and a PRC-117G (VHF/UHF). There is a mountain range between you and the COC.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the distance to the distant station (85 miles).
  2. Consult MCRP 3-40.3C Table 1-1 to determine if VHF Ground Wave can cover 85 miles over mountainous terrain.
  3. Determine the propagation mode required to clear the mountain (Sky Wave).
  4. Select the appropriate frequency band (HF) and justify based on the 'skip' requirements.
Conclusion

Summary: We have defined the MHz boundaries for HF, VHF, and UHF bands and analyzed how Ground Waves and Sky Waves behave. Selecting the right band is the first step in establishing a reliable communication link.

Closing Statement: The mission depends on your ability to analyze the environment and select the right tool for the job. Don't let the terrain dictate your success; let your knowledge of propagation ensure the message gets through.

Lesson 52: Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) Employment

TLO: TLO-052

Introduction

Gain Attention: You are in a 'skip zone'—too far for ground wave to reach, but too close for a standard sky wave to 'skip' back down to you. You are effectively in a communications black hole. NVIS is the technique that allows us to fire a radio wave straight up and have it drop back down like a mortar round, filling that gap and ensuring 100% connectivity in the toughest terrain.

Overview: This lesson covers the definition of NVIS, the critical relationship between frequency and the ionosphere, and the specific antennas required for NVIS operations.

Objectives:

  • ELO-135: Define Near-Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation.
  • ELO-136: Explain the relationship between the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) and NVIS propagation.
  • ELO-137: Identify NVIS-capable antennas.
Body

NVIS Theory and Definition

NVIS is a technique using high-angle radiation to provide regional radio coverage (0-300 miles) per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 4.

  • Radiation Angle: Uses take-off angles of 60 to 90 degrees.
  • Coverage: Eliminates the skip zone, providing 'umbrella' coverage rather than a directional beam.
  • Tactical Advantage: Allows communication from deep valleys or behind dense vegetation.

Frequency Selection and the MUF

Success in NVIS depends entirely on selecting a frequency that the ionosphere will reflect at a steep angle.

  • Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF): The highest frequency that will be reflected back to Earth. Frequencies above the MUF will pass through the ionosphere into space.
  • Critical Frequency: For NVIS, the operating frequency must be below the MUF (typically between 2 and 12 MHz).
  • Diurnal Changes: The MUF changes based on the time of day (higher during the day, lower at night).

NVIS Antennas

Standard vertical whip antennas are poor for NVIS because they radiate energy toward the horizon, not upward.

  • AS-2259/GR: The primary tactical NVIS antenna, featuring crossed dipoles.
  • Half-Wave Dipole: When mounted at low heights (1/8 to 1/4 wavelength above ground), it directs energy vertically.
  • Field Expedients: Bending a vehicle whip antenna horizontally (NVIS 'slap' or 'tie-down') can facilitate high-angle radiation.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your platoon is located in a deep ravine. You must establish an HF link with a unit 40 miles away. You have a PRC-150, a 10-foot whip, and a wire antenna kit.

Practice Steps:

  1. Determine the MUF for the current time of day using provided signal data.
  2. Select an operating frequency approximately 10-20% below the MUF.
  3. Configure the wire antenna as a horizontal half-wave dipole at a height of approximately 15-20 feet to maximize vertical radiation.
  4. Verify the radio's internal coupler achieves a tune, ensuring the high-angle radiation path is established.
Conclusion

Summary: NVIS is a vital HF technique that uses high-angle radiation and frequencies below the MUF to provide regional coverage and overcome terrain masking.

Closing Statement: Mastering NVIS means you are never truly 'cut off' by the terrain. By understanding the ionosphere and proper antenna height, you can maintain the link when every other system fails.

Lesson 53: Grounding of Antenna Systems

TLO: TLO-053

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are in a hide site with a perfect line of sight to your distant end, yet your radio is overheating and your signal is barely breaking squelch. You are literally wasting your transmitter's power by turning it into heat in the dirt. Proper grounding isn't just a safety check; it is the difference between a clear transmission and a fried circuit card.

Overview: This lesson covers the critical requirements for grounding tactical antenna systems, including the purpose of grounding, identification of necessary hardware, and the impact of soil resistance on radio performance.

Objectives:

  • TLO-053: Perform grounding of an antenna system.
  • ELO-138: State the purpose of grounding an antenna system.
  • ELO-139: Identify grounding hardware components.
  • ELO-140: Describe the effects of ground resistance on radio performance.
Body

Purpose and Principles of Grounding

Grounding provides a low-impedance path to the earth, which is essential for the efficient radiation of electromagnetic energy.

  • Minimizing ground resistance ensures that the maximum amount of RF energy is radiated rather than lost.
  • Prevents transmitter power dissipation as heat, which protects internal components from damage (MCRP 3-40.3C, 2-19).
  • Ensures operator safety by preventing chassis electrification.

Grounding Hardware and Installation

Standard USMC tactical radio kits include specific components designed to establish an effective ground.

  • Grounding Stake: The primary interface with the earth.
  • Mallet: Used to drive the stake into the soil.
  • Grounding Strap/Wire: Connects the radio or antenna base to the stake.
  • Standard: The stake must be driven approximately one meter into the earth to reach consistent moisture levels and minimize resistance (MCRP 3-40.3C, 2-20).

Soil Conditions and Resistance

The effectiveness of a ground is highly dependent on the environment.

  • Dry, sandy soil has high resistance, leading to significant energy loss.
  • Moist, loamy soil provides the best conductivity for tactical grounding.
  • Poor grounding leads to reduced signal strength and a higher probability of 'dead spots' in the communication link.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are tasked with establishing a VHF retransmission site on a dry ridgeline. You must ground the OE-254 antenna system to ensure maximum range and equipment longevity.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the grounding stake, strap, and mallet from the SL-3 kit.
  2. Select a location for the stake as close to the antenna base as possible.
  3. Drive the grounding stake into the earth to a depth of approximately one meter.
  4. Clean the contact points on the stake and the antenna base.
  5. Securely attach the grounding strap between the antenna base and the stake.
  6. Verify the connection is tight and free of debris.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the necessity of grounding to prevent heat dissipation and minimize resistance, the hardware required, and the standard of driving stakes to a one-meter depth.

Closing Statement: A radio operator who neglects the ground is an operator who neglects the mission. Ensure your ground is deep and your connections are tight.

Lesson 54: Troubleshooting Manmade Noise Interference

TLO: TLO-054

Introduction

Gain Attention: In a modern tactical environment, the airwaves are crowded. From the hum of a generator to the buzz of overhead power lines, manmade noise can render a million-dollar radio system useless. As a communicator, you must know how to fight through the noise to get the message across.

Overview: This lesson focuses on identifying manmade noise sources and utilizing antenna polarization and placement to mitigate interference and improve signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).

Objectives:

  • TLO-054: Troubleshoot manmade noise interference.
  • ELO-141: Identify common sources of manmade noise.
  • ELO-142: Explain the impact of antenna polarization on signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
  • ELO-143: Differentiate between horizontal and vertical polarization for noise mitigation.
Body

Sources of Manmade Noise

Manmade noise is often the primary limiting factor for VHF and UHF communications in urban or developed areas.

  • Power lines and transformers (constant hum/buzz).
  • Vehicle engines and generators (ignition noise).
  • Electronic devices, computers, and fluorescent lighting (broadband interference).
  • Other tactical radios in close proximity (cosite interference).

Polarization and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)

SNR is the ratio of the desired signal strength to the background noise level. Improving SNR is the goal of all troubleshooting.

  • Matching polarization between the transmitter and receiver maximizes signal reception.
  • Changing polarization can 'reject' interfering signals if the noise source is polarized differently than the desired signal (MCRP 3-40.3C, 2-6).

Mitigation Strategies

When interference occurs, the operator has several tactical options to restore communications.

  • Reorienting antenna polarization: Switching from vertical to horizontal can often drop the noise floor significantly.
  • Relocation: Moving the antenna just a few meters away from a noise source (like a generator) can improve SNR.
  • Narrowband antennas: Utilizing antennas that only accept a specific frequency range to reject out-of-band interference.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your unit is operating near a civilian power substation. Your VHF net is experiencing heavy static, making voice comms unreadable. You are using a vertical whip antenna.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the likely source of interference (power lines).
  2. Monitor the current signal-to-noise ratio on the radio display.
  3. Reorient the antenna from vertical to horizontal polarization.
  4. Coordinate with the distant end to ensure they also switch to horizontal polarization.
  5. Evaluate the change in audio clarity and SNR.
  6. If noise persists, relocate the antenna system to a position where terrain masks the noise source.
Conclusion

Summary: We have identified manmade noise sources and learned how to use antenna polarization and siting to improve the signal-to-noise ratio.

Closing Statement: Do not accept a noisy net as 'just the way it is.' Use your knowledge of polarization and siting to dominate the electromagnetic spectrum.

Lesson 55: Constructing an Artificial Ground (Counterpoise)

TLO: TLO-055

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are deployed to a desert environment with extremely dry, sandy soil. You set up your vertical whip antenna, but your signal is weak and your radio is overheating due to high SWR. In this scenario, the earth is a poor conductor, and your antenna system is incomplete. Without a solid ground, your radio cannot push the signal out. Today, we will learn how to 'create' that ground where nature didn't provide one.

Overview: This lesson covers the theory, calculation, and construction of an artificial ground, known as a counterpoise, to ensure maximum radiation efficiency in poor soil conditions.

Objectives:

  • TLO-055: Construct an artificial ground (counterpoise).
  • ELO-144: Define the purpose and function of a counterpoise.
  • ELO-145: Calculate the required length for counterpoise radials.
Body

Purpose and Function of a Counterpoise

Per MCRP 3-40.3C Section II, a counterpoise is a substitute for an earth ground. It is used when high resistance soil (sand, rock, or dry earth) prevents an effective ground connection.

  • Acts as an artificial capacitance to ground.
  • Facilitates the flow of antenna current by providing a low-impedance return path.
  • Essential for vertical whip or monopole antennas to complete the electrical circuit.

Calculating Radial Length

To ensure resonance and maximum current flow, counterpoise radials must be cut to specific lengths based on the operating frequency.

  • Standard calculation is based on a quarter-wavelength of the operating frequency.
  • Formula: 234 / Frequency (in MHz) = Length in feet.
  • Precision is critical: Radials must be within +/- 2 inches of the calculated length to maintain resonance.

Construction and Deployment

The physical layout of the counterpoise determines its effectiveness in minimizing impedance.

  • Radials should be deployed at the antenna feed point, extending outward like spokes on a wheel.
  • Use conductive material such as copper wire or tactical WD-1/TT wire.
  • Ensure radials are elevated slightly or laid flat on the surface, depending on the specific antenna requirements.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are operating an HF radio at 7.5 MHz in a rocky environment. You must construct a counterpoise for your vertical whip antenna to establish communications with the COC.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the operating frequency (7.5 MHz).
  2. Calculate the required radial length (234 / 7.5 = 31.2 feet).
  3. Measure and cut four radials to 31 feet 2 inches.
  4. Connect the radials to the antenna base (ground side of the mount).
  5. Deploy radials in a 360-degree pattern around the antenna base.
  6. Verify the connection is secure and provides a continuous electrical path.
Conclusion

Summary: We have defined the counterpoise as an artificial ground, calculated radial lengths to within 2 inches of resonance, and discussed the physical construction of the system.

Closing Statement: A Marine's ability to adapt to the environment is what wins battles. When the ground fails you, the counterpoise ensures your message still gets through.

Lesson 56: Installation of Antenna Transmission Lines

TLO: TLO-056

Introduction

Gain Attention: The most powerful radio and the most efficient antenna are useless if the connection between them is flawed. A loose connector or the wrong type of cable can cause up to 90% of your signal to be lost as heat before it ever reaches the antenna. Mastering transmission lines ensures your voice reaches the objective.

Overview: This lesson focuses on identifying transmission line types, understanding the role of baluns, and performing proper installation and weatherproofing of antenna interfaces.

Objectives:

  • TLO-056: Perform the installation of antenna transmission lines.
  • ELO-146: Identify types of transmission lines and their characteristics.
  • ELO-147: Explain the function of a balun in the transmission circuit.
  • ELO-148: Connect transmission line interfaces to the radio and antenna.
Body

Types of Transmission Lines

MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 3 identifies three primary types of lines used in tactical environments.

  • Coaxial Cable: Most common; shielded to prevent interference; 50-ohm impedance (e.g., RG-213).
  • Twin-Lead: Parallel conductors; lower loss than coax but susceptible to nearby metal objects.
  • Open-Wire: Two parallel wires with air insulation; highest efficiency for long-range HF.

The Function of a Balun

A 'Balun' (Balanced to Unbalanced) is a critical component when mixing different types of equipment.

  • Matches an unbalanced line (coax) to a balanced antenna (dipole).
  • Prevents 'line radiation' where the cable itself becomes part of the antenna.
  • Maintains the intended radiation pattern of the antenna system.

Installation Standards

Proper physical connection is the final step in ensuring system integrity.

  • All connectors must be hand-tight; do not use pliers which can damage threads.
  • Weatherproofing (using electrical tape or sealant) is required for long-term installations to prevent moisture ingress.
  • Ensure no sharp bends in the cable, which can change the impedance and cause signal loss.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are tasked with setting up a half-wave dipole antenna using a standard tactical transceiver and coaxial cable.

Practice Steps:

  1. Select the appropriate coaxial cable for the transceiver.
  2. Identify the balun and attach it to the center of the dipole antenna.
  3. Connect the coaxial cable to the unbalanced side of the balun.
  4. Route the cable to the transceiver, avoiding sharp 90-degree bends.
  5. Connect the cable to the radio's antenna port, ensuring it is hand-tight.
  6. Apply weatherproofing tape to the outdoor balun-to-cable connection.
Conclusion

Summary: We have identified the characteristics of coax and wire lines, explained how baluns maintain radiation patterns, and practiced the standards for secure, weatherproof connections.

Closing Statement: Attention to detail in your connections is the difference between a clear transmission and total radio silence. Treat your transmission lines with the same care as your weapon system.

Lesson 57: Employment of the AS-2259/GR Antenna

TLO: TLO-057

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are operating in a deep valley with 2,000-foot ridgelines on all sides. Your standard whip antenna can't clear the terrain, and your distant station is only 50 miles away—too close for traditional skywave but too far for ground wave. This is the 'skip zone.' The AS-2259/GR is your solution, using Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) to 'bounce' your signal off the ionosphere and straight back down, effectively turning the sky into your repeater.

Overview: This lesson covers the theory of NVIS propagation, the identification of AS-2259/GR components, and the step-by-step assembly of the antenna system to establish reliable HF communications in restrictive terrain.

Objectives:

  • TLO-057: Demonstrate the employment of an AS-2259/GR antenna.
  • ELO-149: Explain the concept of Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) propagation.
  • ELO-150: Identify all components of the AS-2259/GR antenna kit.
  • ELO-151: Assemble the AS-2259/GR antenna mast and radiating elements.
Body

NVIS Propagation Theory

NVIS is a technique used to provide reliable communications over a range of 0 to 300 miles. It utilizes a high take-off angle (near 90 degrees) to direct the signal to the ionosphere, where it is reflected back to Earth at a similar angle.

  • Overcomes terrain obstructions like mountains or dense vegetation.
  • Eliminates the 'skip zone' where ground waves die out and skywaves have not yet returned.
  • Requires frequencies usually between 2 and 12 MHz depending on atmospheric conditions.

AS-2259/GR Component Identification

The AS-2259/GR is a tactical, man-portable antenna kit designed specifically for NVIS. Operators must ensure all components are present and serviceable before deployment.

  • Base Matching Unit: Provides the interface between the radio and the antenna.
  • Mast Sections: Seven interlocking sections that provide the vertical structure.
  • Radiating Elements: Four wire elements that serve as both the electrical antenna and the guy wires.
  • Carrying Bag: Used for transport and storage of all kit components.

Assembly and Safety Procedures

Assembly must follow a specific sequence to ensure structural integrity and operator safety. The antenna is typically 15 feet tall when fully assembled.

  • Site Selection: Choose a level area free of overhead power lines.
  • Base Setup: Secure the base matching unit and begin interlocking mast sections.
  • Element Deployment: Extend the four radiating elements at 90-degree intervals.
  • Safety: Ensure no personnel are touching the antenna during transmission due to RF burn hazards.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your unit is established in a mountain patrol base. You are tasked with establishing an HF link back to the Combat Operations Center (COC) located 45 miles away. Terrain prevents line-of-sight. You must deploy the AS-2259/GR to facilitate NVIS communications.

Practice Steps:

  1. Inventory the AS-2259/GR kit to ensure all components are serviceable.
  2. Select a suitable site and clear debris.
  3. Assemble the mast sections and attach the base matching unit.
  4. Deploy and stake the four radiating elements at 90-degree intervals.
  5. Connect the RF cable to the HF radio and perform a built-in test (BIT).
  6. Establish a voice check with the distant station.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the fundamentals of NVIS propagation, identified the critical components of the AS-2259/GR, and practiced the assembly of the system. Understanding NVIS is the difference between being 'blacked out' by terrain and maintaining critical C2.

Closing Statement: The AS-2259/GR is a force multiplier in mountainous or jungle environments. Master its assembly, and you ensure your unit's voice is always heard, regardless of the terrain.

Lesson 58: Employment of the OE-254 Antenna

TLO: TLO-058

Introduction

Gain Attention: Your standard vehicle whip antenna is rated for about 15-30 miles under ideal conditions. But what happens when the convoy moves 40 miles out? To maintain the net, you need height and gain. The OE-254 antenna extends your VHF range significantly, ensuring that distance doesn't become a barrier to mission success.

Overview: This lesson focuses on the OE-254 antenna system, covering component identification and the technical procedures for erecting the mast safely to support VHF line-of-sight communications.

Objectives:

  • TLO-058: Demonstrate the employment of an OE-254 antenna.
  • ELO-152: Identify the components of an OE-254 antenna kit.
  • ELO-153: Perform the assembly and erection of the OE-254 antenna.
Body

OE-254 System Components

The OE-254 is a broadband, omnidirectional antenna system operating in the 30-88 MHz range. It does not require tuning, making it ideal for frequency-hopping nets.

  • Feedcone and Radiating Elements: The 'top' of the antenna that handles the signal.
  • Mast Sections: 11 tubular sections used to reach a height of approximately 30 feet.
  • Guy Wires and Stakes: Used to stabilize the mast against wind and gravity.
  • Base Stake: The foundation point for the mast assembly.

Assembly and Erection Procedures

Erecting a 30-foot mast requires coordination and adherence to safety standards to prevent equipment damage or injury.

  • Ground Assembly: The feedcone and elements are assembled on the ground before the mast is raised.
  • Guy Wire Spacing: Guy wires must be secured at 120-degree intervals to provide equal tension.
  • Verticality: The mast must be perfectly vertical to ensure omnidirectional coverage and structural stability.
  • Cable Management: Ensure the coaxial cable is not kinked or pinched during the lift.
Practical Application

Scenario: The Platoon is establishing a static Observation Post (OP). You are required to increase the range of the VHF net to reach the Company HQ. You have been provided an OE-254 kit and must erect it within 15 minutes.

Practice Steps:

  1. Layout all components and verify serviceability per MCRP 3-40.3C.
  2. Assemble the feedcone and attach the three upper radiating elements.
  3. Connect the coaxial cable to the feedcone.
  4. Assemble mast sections and attach guy wires to the guy rings.
  5. Erect the antenna using the 'walk-up' or 'vertical' method as a team.
  6. Secure guy wires to stakes at 120-degree intervals and tension the lines.
  7. Connect to the VHF radio and verify signal strength.
Conclusion

Summary: We have identified the components of the OE-254 and demonstrated the proper techniques for its assembly and erection. This antenna is the standard for extending VHF range in the Marine Corps.

Closing Statement: A radio is only as good as its antenna. By mastering the OE-254, you provide your commander with the extended reach necessary for modern distributed operations.

Lesson 59: Planning the Siting of an Antenna Farm

TLO: TLO-059

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine your unit is established in a hide site, but your radio signature is so concentrated and poorly managed that it glows like a beacon on enemy electronic warfare displays. A poorly planned antenna farm doesn't just cause signal interference; it provides the enemy with the exact coordinates of your Command Post (CP). Proper siting is the difference between mission success and being targeted by indirect fire before the first SITREP is even sent.

Overview: This lesson covers the tactical, technical, and doctrinal requirements for siting an antenna farm. We will discuss how to balance the need for signal radiation with the requirement for concealment and how to calculate the necessary separation between antennas to prevent co-site interference.

Objectives:

  • ELO-154: Identify tactical, technical, and doctrinal siting considerations for an antenna farm.
  • ELO-155: Determine the required separation distances between antennas.
  • ELO-156: Analyze terrain for the placement of an antenna farm.
Body

Siting Considerations

Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 8, siting must balance three primary categories of considerations to ensure survivability and connectivity.

  • Tactical: Focus on concealment from ground and air observation, use of natural cover, and physical security of the site.
  • Doctrinal: Placement relative to the Command Post (Main, Tactical, or Rear) and accessibility for maintenance personnel.
  • Technical: Avoiding man-made noise sources (generators, power lines) and ensuring the ground conductivity supports the frequency bands in use.

Antenna Separation and Layout

To minimize co-site interference, antennas must be separated based on their frequency and power output. This prevents 'de-sensing' receivers and ensures clear communication.

  • Vertical Separation: Placing antennas at different heights to reduce coupling.
  • Horizontal Separation: Maintaining physical distance between antennas operating in the same frequency band.
  • Frequency Separation: Ensuring assigned frequencies are not too close to each other (typically 10% separation for VHF).

Terrain Analysis for CIS

Terrain selection is driven by the wave propagation characteristics of the equipment being used.

  • Line of Sight (LOS): VHF and UHF systems require high ground with clear paths to distant stations.
  • Masking: Using hills or vegetation to shield the antenna farm from enemy direction-finding (DF) while maintaining a path for friendly signals.
  • HF NVIS: Requires relatively flat areas without overhead obstructions to allow for high-angle radiation.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are the CIS Chief for an infantry battalion. You have been provided a 1:50,000 scale map and a list of 12 radio nets (4 HF, 6 VHF, 2 UHF). You must select a site for the antenna farm that is within 300 meters of the CP but remains concealed from a known enemy observation post on a nearby ridge.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify potential high ground for VHF/UHF LOS requirements.
  2. Evaluate vegetation and depressions for tactical concealment.
  3. Sketch an antenna farm layout showing at least 15 meters of separation between VHF antennas.
  4. Identify power line hazards or man-made noise sources on the map to avoid.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the critical factors in siting an antenna farm, including the tactical need for concealment, the technical requirement for antenna separation, and the analysis of terrain to support LOS and NVIS propagation.

Closing Statement: A professional CIS plan is invisible to the enemy but crystal clear to the commander. Master these siting principles to keep your unit connected and alive.

Lesson 60: Construction of a Half-Wave Dipole Antenna

TLO: TLO-060

Introduction

Gain Attention: You are 300 miles from the nearest relay, and your standard vehicle whip antenna cannot break through the atmospheric noise. You have a spool of wire, some insulators, and a radio. In the next hour, you will learn how to turn those raw materials into a high-gain antenna that can reach across the battlespace using the principles of resonance.

Overview: This lesson provides the mathematical and practical steps to construct a field-expedient half-wave dipole antenna. We will calculate the length based on frequency, assemble the components, and verify the antenna's performance using VSWR.

Objectives:

  • ELO-157: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole antenna.
  • ELO-158: Assemble the components of a field-expedient dipole.
  • ELO-159: Verify the resonance of the antenna.
Body

Antenna Length Calculation

The physical length of an antenna must correspond to the wavelength of the assigned frequency to achieve resonance.

  • The standard formula for a half-wave dipole in feet is: 468 divided by the frequency in MHz.
  • Example: For a frequency of 10 MHz, the total length is 46.8 feet.
  • Each 'leg' of the dipole is half of the total length (23.4 feet).

Assembly and Construction

Proper assembly ensures the antenna is durable and electrically sound.

  • Wire: Use copper or WD-1/TT field wire.
  • Insulators: Use glass, plastic, or dry wood to prevent the signal from grounding out at the ends.
  • Feed Line: The coaxial cable must be attached at the center, with the center conductor to one leg and the shield to the other.

Verification of Resonance

Once constructed, the antenna must be tested to ensure it is efficiently radiating energy rather than reflecting it back into the radio.

  • Voltage Standing Wave Ratio (VSWR) measures this efficiency.
  • A ratio of 1:1 is perfect; 3:1 is the maximum acceptable limit for most tactical radios.
  • High VSWR indicates the antenna is the wrong length or has a poor connection, which can damage the radio's power amplifier.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your team is assigned a primary HF frequency of 7.5 MHz. You must construct a half-wave dipole antenna using the provided field kit and establish a link with the distant station.

Practice Steps:

  1. Calculate the total length of the antenna (468 / 7.5 = 62.4 feet).
  2. Measure and cut two lengths of wire, each 31.2 feet long.
  3. Attach the wires to the center insulator and connect the coaxial feed line.
  4. Attach end insulators and hoist the antenna into the air using para-cord.
  5. Connect the radio and perform a VSWR check to ensure a reading of 3:1 or less.
Conclusion

Summary: You now know how to calculate the length of a dipole, assemble it from field-expedient materials, and verify that it is tuned to your operating frequency.

Closing Statement: The ability to build an antenna from scratch is the hallmark of a proficient radio operator. When the standard equipment fails, your knowledge of antenna fundamentals ensures the message still gets through.

Lesson 61: VHF/UHF Reflected Wave Communications

TLO: TLO-061

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are operating in a dense urban environment or a deep mountain valley. You have a clear mission, but a massive concrete structure or a granite cliff face is standing directly between you and your distant station, completely severing your Line of Sight (LOS). In the VHF and UHF bands, we are taught that LOS is king, but when the king falls, the reflected wave becomes your best friend. Understanding how to 'bounce' your signal off the environment can be the difference between mission success and total comms blackout.

Overview: This lesson covers the technical principles of reflected wave propagation and the practical application of using environmental surfaces to maintain VHF/UHF communications when direct line-of-sight is obstructed.

Objectives:

  • TLO-061: Demonstrate communications using reflected waves.
  • ELO-160: Identify the principles of reflected wave propagation.
  • ELO-161: Describe the characteristics of suitable reflecting surfaces for VHF/UHF signals.
Body

Principles of Reflected Wave Propagation

Per MCRP 3-40.3C Chapter 1, radio waves behave similarly to light waves when they encounter a surface. When a VHF/UHF wave hits a reflecting surface, it creates an incident wave and a reflected wave.

  • The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
  • Reflection occurs when the surface is large compared to the wavelength of the signal.
  • VHF/UHF waves are particularly susceptible to reflection due to their shorter wavelengths.

Characteristics of Suitable Reflecting Surfaces

Not all surfaces are created equal. To effectively bounce a signal, the operator must identify surfaces that minimize absorption and maximize reflection.

  • Conductivity: Metallic surfaces (water towers, hangars) are the most efficient reflectors.
  • Density: Solid rock faces and concrete buildings provide high reflectivity compared to vegetation.
  • Surface Smoothness: The surface must be relatively smooth in relation to the wavelength to avoid scattering (diffraction).
  • Size: The surface must be several wavelengths wide and tall to act as an effective mirror for the signal.

Antenna Orientation for Reflected Waves

To use a reflected wave, the operator must deviate from standard 'pointing' procedures.

  • Direct the antenna toward the reflecting object rather than the distant station.
  • Coordinate with the receiving station to also orient their antenna toward the same reflecting point.
  • Maintain proper polarization (usually vertical for tactical VHF) to ensure signal consistency.
Practical Application

Scenario: The unit is positioned behind a large hill that blocks direct LOS to the Combat Operations Center (COC). A large metal warehouse is visible to the North, which has a clear view of both your position and the COC.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the warehouse as the primary reflecting surface based on material and location.
  2. Calculate the approximate angle required to hit the surface so the reflection angle points toward the COC.
  3. Orient the VHF whip or directional antenna toward the warehouse.
  4. Attempt to establish contact and make small adjustments to the antenna azimuth to peak the signal strength.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered how VHF/UHF signals can be reflected off man-made and natural structures to overcome LOS obstructions. We identified that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection and that dense, conductive surfaces make the best reflectors.

Closing Statement: In the modern battlespace, you won't always have a clear line of sight. Master the reflected wave, and you ensure that terrain never dictates your ability to communicate.

Lesson 62: HF Antenna Selection for Sky Wave Propagation

TLO: TLO-062

Introduction

Gain Attention: You are tasked with establishing a high-frequency (HF) circuit to a unit 200 miles away. You have a radio, a wire kit, and a ticking clock. If you choose an antenna with a take-off angle that is too low, your signal will skip right over the target. If it's too high, it might not have the range. In HF communications, your antenna is your most critical piece of software—select the wrong one, and you are just talking to yourself.

Overview: This lesson focuses on the relationship between take-off angles, circuit distances, and the selection of HF antennas using MCRP 3-40.3C standardized data.

Objectives:

  • TLO-062: Determine the appropriate HF antenna for sky wave propagation.
  • ELO-162: Explain the relationship between take-off angle and circuit distance.
  • ELO-163: Interpret antenna selection data from Table 4-1.
  • ELO-164: Compare antenna characteristics regarding gain and directivity.
Body

Take-Off Angle and Circuit Distance

The take-off angle is the angle above the horizon at which an antenna radiates the majority of its energy. This angle determines where the signal will return to earth after reflecting off the ionosphere.

  • High Take-Off Angles (60-90 degrees): Used for Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) to cover short ranges (0-300 miles) and overcome terrain masking.
  • Low Take-Off Angles (less than 30 degrees): Used for long-distance communications (300+ miles) to maximize skip distance.
  • The height of the antenna above ground directly influences the take-off angle.

Interpreting Table 4-1 (Antenna Selection)

MCRP 3-40.3C Table 4-1 provides a standardized matrix for selecting antennas based on distance and time of day.

  • Distance Categories: Short (0-300 miles), Medium (300-1000 miles), Long (1000+ miles).
  • Time of Day: Ionospheric layers change between day and night, requiring different frequency and antenna considerations.
  • Antenna Recommendations: Identifies specific types like the AS-2259, Dipole, or Inverted Vee based on these variables.

Comparing Gain and Directivity

Different antennas provide different levels of gain (signal strength) and directivity (concentration of energy).

  • Omnidirectional: Best for nets with stations in multiple directions (e.g., Vertical Whip).
  • Bidirectional: Concentrates energy in two directions (e.g., Half-Wave Dipole).
  • Directional: Maximum gain toward a specific station (e.g., Sloping Vee or Rhombic).
  • Gain vs. Complexity: Higher gain antennas often require more space and setup time.
Practical Application

Scenario: Mission: Establish a 150-mile HF circuit during daylight hours. You have a standard wire antenna kit and an AS-2259/GR. Terrain is heavily wooded.

Practice Steps:

  1. Consult MCRP 3-40.3C Table 4-1 for the 0-300 mile range.
  2. Identify that a high take-off angle (NVIS) is required for this distance.
  3. Compare the AS-2259 (NVIS specific) against a Horizontal Dipole.
  4. Select the AS-2259/GR or a Dipole at a height of 1/4 wavelength or less to ensure the required take-off angle.
  5. Justify the selection based on the need to clear the surrounding vegetation and hit the 150-mile target.
Conclusion

Summary: We have analyzed how take-off angles dictate the skip distance of an HF signal and how to use Table 4-1 to select the right antenna for the mission. We also compared gain and directivity to ensure the signal reaches the intended recipient.

Closing Statement: HF is an art backed by science. By mastering antenna selection, you turn the ionosphere into a tool rather than an obstacle.

Lesson 63: Construction of Field-Expedient Antennas

TLO: TLO-063

Introduction

Gain Attention: You are operating in a dense jungle environment and your standard vehicle whip antenna has been sheared off by heavy vegetation. You are out of range for your manpack's standard antenna, and a CASEVAC request needs to be transmitted immediately. In this moment, your ability to turn a roll of WD-1/TT wire and some plastic spoons into a functional antenna is the only thing that will get that bird in the air. Field expediency is not just a 'nice to have' skill; it is a survival requirement for the Marine communicator.

Overview: This lesson covers the fundamental principles of constructing field-expedient antennas using MCRP 3-40.3C. We will focus on identifying necessary components, calculating precise lengths for specific frequencies, and applying proper insulation techniques to ensure signal radiation.

Objectives:

  • TLO-063: Construct a field-expedient antenna.
  • ELO-165: Calculate the physical length of a wire antenna.
  • ELO-166: Identify the components required for a field-expedient antenna.
  • ELO-167: Apply proper insulation and support techniques.
Body

Antenna Components and Materials

A field-expedient antenna requires three primary components to function effectively: the radiator, the transmission line, and insulators.

  • Radiator: The active element (usually wire) that emits the radio frequency energy.
  • Transmission Line: The medium (coaxial cable or twin-lead) that carries energy from the radio to the antenna.
  • Insulators: Non-conductive materials (plastic, glass, or dry wood) used to prevent the signal from grounding into supports like trees or poles.

Calculating Antenna Length

To achieve resonance, the antenna must be cut to a specific length based on the assigned frequency. For a half-wave dipole, the standard formula is used to ensure maximum power transfer.

  • Formula: Length in feet = 468 / Frequency in MHz.
  • Example: For a frequency of 14.2 MHz, the total length is approximately 33 feet (16.5 feet per element).
  • Accuracy: Calculations must be accurate to within 1 inch to maintain a low Standing Wave Ratio (SWR).

Insulation and Support Techniques

Proper mounting is critical. An antenna that touches a wet tree limb or the ground will short out, causing the radio to lose power or sustain damage.

  • Height: Antennas should be mounted as high as possible to achieve the required radiation pattern and clear obstacles.
  • Isolation: Use field-expedient insulators (buttons, plastic scraps, or dry wood) at the ends of the radiator to separate it from the support ropes.
  • Orientation: Ensure the antenna is oriented (broadside) toward the receiving station for maximum signal strength.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your unit is established in a temporary patrol base. You are assigned a frequency of 35.50 MHz (VHF). You must construct a center-fed half-wave dipole using a field antenna kit and available trees for support.

Practice Steps:

  1. Calculate the total length of the radiator using the formula (468 / 35.5).
  2. Measure and cut two equal lengths of wire (each representing 1/4 wavelength).
  3. Identify and inspect insulators for cracks or conductivity.
  4. Attach the radiator wires to the center insulator and the transmission line.
  5. Secure the ends of the radiator to support ropes using insulators.
  6. Hoist the antenna into the trees, ensuring it does not touch branches or the ground.
  7. Connect to the radio and perform a radio check.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the identification of antenna components, the mathematical calculation of antenna length based on frequency, and the physical techniques required to insulate and support a field-expedient antenna.

Closing Statement: The difference between a successful mission and a communications failure often comes down to the operator's technical proficiency. Master these calculations and construction techniques now so you can employ them when the tactical situation is at its worst.

Lesson 64: Troubleshooting and Field Repair of Antenna Systems

TLO: TLO-064

Introduction

Gain Attention: In the heat of an engagement, antennas are often the first things to break. Shrapnel, high winds, and vehicle movement can easily snap a whip or sever a wire. If you cannot repair your antenna in the field, you are effectively out of the fight. A Marine who can troubleshoot and perform a Western Union splice under pressure is an invaluable asset to any maneuver element.

Overview: This lesson focuses on identifying common antenna failures and performing field-expedient repairs to restore electrical continuity and structural integrity to antenna systems per MCRP 3-40.3C.

Objectives:

  • TLO-064: Troubleshoot antenna components for field repair.
  • ELO-168: Identify common types of damage to whip, wire, and mast components.
  • ELO-169: Describe field repair techniques for wire and whip antennas.
  • ELO-170: Perform a western union splice on antenna wire.
Body

Identifying Antenna System Damage

Troubleshooting begins with a visual inspection of the entire system from the radio connector to the tip of the antenna.

  • Whip Antennas: Look for cracks at the base, snapped sections, or corrosion at the joints.
  • Wire Antennas: Check for frayed insulation, severed conductors, or grounded wires.
  • Masts and Guys: Inspect for bent sections, frayed guy lines, or loose tensioners that affect stability.

Field Repair Principles

The goal of any field repair is to restore two things: electrical continuity and mechanical strength.

  • Electrical Continuity: The signal must have a clear, low-resistance path to travel. Use solder or tight mechanical splices.
  • Mechanical Strength: The repair must be able to withstand the tension of being hoisted or the vibration of a moving vehicle.
  • Weatherproofing: Use electrical tape or heat shrink to prevent moisture from corroding the repair site.

The Western Union Splice

The Western Union splice is the standard military method for joining two pieces of antenna wire because it provides excellent conductivity and will not pull apart under tension.

  • Preparation: Strip approximately 4-6 inches of insulation from both ends of the wire.
  • The Twist: Cross the wires and wrap each end tightly around the standing part of the opposite wire (at least 5-7 turns).
  • Finishing: Ensure the wraps are tight and close together to maximize surface contact.
Practical Application

Scenario: During a movement to contact, a low-hanging branch has severed the wire antenna used for your long-range HF net. You must troubleshoot the system, identify the break, and perform a permanent field repair to restore communications.

Practice Steps:

  1. Perform a visual inspection of the antenna system to locate the break.
  2. Retrieve the severed ends of the antenna wire.
  3. Strip the insulation from the wire ends using a multi-tool or knife.
  4. Execute a Western Union splice, ensuring at least five tight wraps on each side.
  5. Test the mechanical strength of the splice by applying moderate tension.
  6. Seal the splice with electrical tape to prevent corrosion.
  7. Re-hoist the antenna and verify electrical continuity with a radio check.
Conclusion

Summary: We have discussed how to identify damage across various antenna types, the principles of maintaining continuity and strength, and the specific steps to perform a Western Union splice.

Closing Statement: Equipment will fail, but the mission cannot. Your ability to troubleshoot and repair your gear ensures that the Commander's intent is always heard, regardless of the conditions on the ground.

Lesson 65: Transmission Line Installation and Management

TLO: TLO-065

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are in a high-stakes environment where every word of a SITREP matters, but your million-dollar radio system is failing because of a five-dollar connector. You can have the best radio and the perfect antenna, but if the transmission line between them is poorly installed, your signal will dissipate as heat before it ever leaves the wire. Today, we ensure that power reaches the air.

Overview: This lesson covers the selection, characteristics, and installation of transmission lines, focusing on impedance matching, minimizing SWR, and proper physical connection techniques per MCRP 3-40.3C.

Objectives:

  • TLO-065: Implement transmission line installation.
  • ELO-171: Identify the characteristics of coaxial and twin-lead transmission lines.
  • ELO-172: Explain the effects of attenuation and Standing Wave Ratio (SWR) on radio performance.
  • ELO-173: Connect transmission lines using appropriate connectors or baluns.
Body

Transmission Line Characteristics

Transmission lines are the vital link between the transceiver and the antenna. Understanding their electrical properties is essential for system efficiency.

  • Coaxial Cable: Most common in the Marine Corps (e.g., RG-213, RG-58). Consists of a center conductor, dielectric insulator, shield, and outer jacket. Standard impedance is typically 50 ohms.
  • Twin-Lead: Consists of two parallel conductors. It has higher impedance (typically 300 ohms) and lower loss than coax but is more susceptible to interference and environmental factors.
  • Impedance Matching: The characteristic impedance of the line must match the radio and the antenna to ensure maximum power transfer.

Attenuation and Standing Wave Ratio (SWR)

Improper installation leads to signal degradation and potential hardware failure.

  • Attenuation: The gradual loss of signal strength as it travels through the line, measured in decibels (dB). Caused by resistance in the wire and dielectric losses.
  • SWR: A measure of how much power is reflected back to the transmitter. High SWR (above 3:1) indicates a mismatch, reducing radiated power and potentially damaging the radio's final power amplifier.
  • Power Loss: Energy not radiated is converted to heat within the transmission line or the radio.

Installation and Connection Techniques

Physical security and weatherproofing are the primary defenses against signal leakage and line degradation.

  • Connectors: Use of BNC, N-type, or PL-259 connectors. Ensure they are tight and free of corrosion.
  • Baluns: Used when connecting a balanced antenna (like a dipole) to an unbalanced line (coax) to maintain the radiation pattern and prevent line radiation.
  • Weather-Sealing: Use of silicone tape or electrical sealant on outdoor connections to prevent moisture ingress, which causes rapid attenuation and cable rot.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are tasked with setting up a temporary base station. You have been provided with an HF radio, a dipole antenna, and a roll of RG-213 coaxial cable. You must prepare the line and connect the system for immediate operation.

Practice Steps:

  1. Select the correct transmission line (coax) for the 50-ohm radio output.
  2. Inspect connectors for physical damage or shorts.
  3. Connect the coax to the antenna using a 1:1 balun to ensure a balanced feed.
  4. Secure all connections with weather-sealing tape.
  5. Route the cable to avoid sharp bends or proximity to power lines.
  6. Perform a radio check and monitor the SWR meter to ensure a reading below 1.5:1.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the differences between coaxial and twin-lead lines, the critical nature of impedance matching to prevent high SWR, and the technical requirements for physical installation.

Closing Statement: A Marine's ability to communicate is only as reliable as the cable connecting their gear. Master these connections, and you ensure the message gets through every time.

Lesson 66: Construction of Field-Expedient Vertical Half-Rhombic Antennas

TLO: TLO-066

Introduction

Gain Attention: You are operating in a valley and need to hit a distant station 400 miles away, but your standard whip antenna is failing to clear the ridgeline. By using a few hundred feet of wire and a single resistor, you can build a directional 'powerhouse' that focuses your signal exactly where it needs to go. This is the Vertical Half-Rhombic.

Overview: This lesson provides the technical procedures for calculating, aligning, and constructing a field-expedient vertical half-rhombic antenna to achieve directional gain in the HF band.

Objectives:

  • TLO-066: Construct a field-expedient vertical half-rhombic antenna.
  • ELO-174: Calculate the required length for a half-rhombic antenna wire.
  • ELO-175: Align the antenna's major axis toward the distant station.
  • ELO-176: Install a terminating resistor at the end of the antenna wire.
Body

Antenna Theory and Calculation

The vertical half-rhombic is a long-wire antenna that uses the ground to complete its electrical circuit, creating a directional radiation pattern.

  • Wavelength Calculation: Use the formula (492 / Frequency in MHz) to find the half-wavelength in feet.
  • Leg Length: For a half-rhombic, each leg should typically be at least one full wavelength for effective gain.
  • Height Requirements: The center support (mast) must be high enough to maintain the required angle for the desired take-off angle.

Orientation and Alignment

Because the half-rhombic is highly directional, precise alignment is mandatory for successful communication.

  • Major Axis: The line running from the feed point through the mast to the termination point.
  • Compass Calibration: Use a lensatic compass to determine the azimuth to the distant station.
  • Tolerance: The antenna must be aligned within 5 degrees of the target azimuth to ensure the main lobe of the radiation pattern covers the receiving station.

Termination and Grounding

The terminating resistor is what differentiates a directional antenna from a bi-directional one.

  • Resistor Value: A non-inductive resistor of 500-600 ohms is required.
  • Function: The resistor absorbs the energy that would otherwise reflect back, making the antenna 'non-resonant' and unidirectional.
  • Grounding: The resistor must be connected to a high-quality ground (ground rod or counterpoise) at the far end of the antenna to complete the circuit.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your unit is established in a patrol base and requires long-haul HF communications to a higher headquarters located at an azimuth of 045 degrees. You are provided with a spool of WD-1/TT wire, a 600-ohm resistor, and a 30-foot mast.

Practice Steps:

  1. Calculate the wire length based on the assigned frequency of 7.5 MHz.
  2. Measure and cut the wire to the calculated length (+/- 1 inch).
  3. Use a lensatic compass to stake out the 045-degree azimuth line.
  4. Erect the center mast and attach the wire, ensuring it forms the 'V' shape in the vertical plane.
  5. Install the 600-ohm resistor at the distant end of the wire.
  6. Drive a ground rod and attach the other end of the resistor to it.
  7. Connect the feed point to the radio and verify the directional orientation.
Conclusion

Summary: We have practiced the mathematical calculation of antenna legs, the use of the lensatic compass for directional alignment, and the installation of the terminating resistor to ensure unidirectional gain.

Closing Statement: The vertical half-rhombic is one of the most effective field-expedient tools in a communicator's arsenal. When the terrain is against you, use the physics of the half-rhombic to win the frequency.

Lesson 67: Antenna Orientation and Polarization

TLO: TLO-067

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are in a high-stakes environment where every second counts. You have a clear line of sight to your distant station, your batteries are fresh, and your frequency is correct, yet your signal is barely readable. You rotate your antenna 90 degrees, and suddenly the signal is crystal clear. That simple adjustment is the power of understanding antenna polarization.

Overview: This lesson covers the fundamental concepts of antenna polarization, the specific characteristics of vertical and horizontal fields, and how to orient antennas to achieve maximum signal strength per MCRP 3-40.3C.

Objectives:

  • TLO-067: Demonstrate antenna orientation for polarization.
  • ELO-177: Define antenna polarization.
  • ELO-178: Describe the advantages of vertical and horizontal polarization.
Body

Defining Antenna Polarization

Polarization is the orientation of the electric field (E-plane) as it leaves the antenna in relation to the earth's surface. It is a critical factor in antenna-to-antenna communication.

  • The electric field determines the polarization.
  • If the electric field is parallel to the earth, it is horizontally polarized.
  • If the electric field is perpendicular to the earth, it is vertically polarized.
  • For maximum signal transfer, both the transmitting and receiving antennas must have the same polarization.

Vertical Polarization Characteristics

Vertical polarization is widely used in tactical environments, particularly with whip antennas and mobile communications.

  • Advantage: Provides omnidirectional (360-degree) coverage.
  • Advantage: More effective for ground wave propagation over long distances.
  • Disadvantage: More susceptible to manmade noise, which is often vertically polarized.

Horizontal Polarization Characteristics

Horizontal polarization is frequently used in high frequency (HF) sky wave communications and fixed-site installations.

  • Advantage: Less susceptible to manmade interference (e.g., vehicle ignitions).
  • Advantage: Effective for Near Vertical Incidence Skywave (NVIS) to communicate over obstacles.
  • Requirement: Requires more space and support structures (masts/trees) than vertical whips.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are tasked with establishing a VHF link between two stationary command posts separated by 15 kilometers of rolling terrain. You have been issued two OE-254 antenna systems.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the polarization of the distant station's antenna.
  2. Assemble the OE-254 antenna system according to technical manuals.
  3. Orient the antenna elements to match the polarization of the distant station (Vertical for standard VHF tactical nets).
  4. Conduct a radio check to verify signal strength.
  5. Rotate the antenna 90 degrees to observe the 'cross-polarization' effect and the resulting signal degradation.
Conclusion

Summary: We have defined antenna polarization as the orientation of the electric field relative to the earth. We compared vertical polarization, ideal for mobile ground waves, with horizontal polarization, which excels in reducing manmade noise and supporting sky wave propagation.

Closing Statement: Mastering antenna orientation ensures that you maximize your equipment's potential, ensuring the MAGTF maintains the critical comms link required for mission success.

Lesson 68: Troubleshooting Manmade Noise Interference

TLO: TLO-068

Introduction

Gain Attention: In a modern tactical environment, the enemy isn't the only thing trying to jam your signal. Your own generators, vehicles, and even poorly shielded power lines can create a 'wall of noise' that renders your multi-million dollar radio system useless. Knowing how to fight through this manmade noise is a requirement for every radio operator.

Overview: This lesson focuses on identifying manmade noise sources, understanding their impact on the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and applying mitigation techniques to restore reliable communications.

Objectives:

  • TLO-068: Troubleshoot manmade noise interference.
  • ELO-179: Identify common sources of manmade noise.
  • ELO-180: Explain the impact of noise on the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR).
  • ELO-181: Determine mitigation techniques for noise reduction.
Body

Sources of Manmade Noise

Manmade noise is caused by the discharge of electrical energy. It is most prevalent in urban areas or near industrial/military hubs.

  • Power lines and transformers (arcing or corona discharge).
  • Vehicle ignition systems and alternators.
  • Electric motors and generators.
  • Computers, switching power supplies, and other digital electronic equipment.

Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)

The SNR is the relationship between the strength of the desired signal and the level of background noise (the noise floor).

  • A high SNR means the signal is much stronger than the noise, resulting in clear audio/data.
  • A low SNR occurs when the noise floor rises, 'masking' the signal and making it unreadable.
  • Increasing transmitter power is one way to improve SNR, but reducing the noise floor at the receiver is often more effective.

Mitigation and Troubleshooting Techniques

When interference is detected, operators must systematically apply techniques to reduce the noise floor.

  • Re-siting: Move the antenna away from the noise source (e.g., move 50 meters away from a generator).
  • Polarization Change: If the noise is vertically polarized (common for power lines), switching to horizontal polarization can significantly reduce interference.
  • Grounding: Ensure the radio and antenna system are properly grounded to drain off stray electromagnetic energy.
  • Physical Shielding: Use terrain or buildings to block the path between the noise source and the antenna.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your radio team is co-located with a logistics hub. You are experiencing heavy static on your HF net, coinciding with the operation of a large mobile generator 10 meters from your antenna.

Practice Steps:

  1. Monitor the radio and identify the specific type of interference (pulsing vs. constant hum).
  2. Measure the signal quality with the generator running versus when it is momentarily shut down.
  3. Calculate the approximate SNR based on the radio's signal strength indicator.
  4. Relocate the antenna to a distance at least 30-50 meters from the generator and power lines.
  5. Verify the improvement in SNR and conduct a radio check with the distant station.
Conclusion

Summary: We have identified that manmade noise from vehicles and power lines can severely degrade our Signal-to-Noise Ratio. By understanding how the noise floor masks our signals, we can apply mitigation techniques like re-siting, grounding, and polarization shifts.

Closing Statement: A radio operator who can troubleshoot noise is an asset to any unit. Don't just accept a bad signal—find the source, mitigate the noise, and get the message through.

Lesson 69: Antenna Selection Criteria

TLO: TLO-069

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are part of a Quick Reaction Force (QRF) inserted into a deep valley. Your mission depends on maintaining a link with the Combat Operations Center (COC) 150 miles away. You have an HF radio, but if you simply throw up a standard whip antenna, your signal will likely be absorbed by the canyon walls or shoot straight into space and never return. Selecting the right antenna isn't just a technical task; it is the difference between a successful extraction and being cut off from support.

Overview: This lesson covers the critical factors in selecting the correct antenna for tactical communications, focusing on the relationship between frequency bands, range requirements, and antenna radiation patterns as defined in MCRP 3-40.3C.

Objectives:

  • TLO-069: Given a mission requirement, an assigned frequency (HF, VHF, or UHF), and a specified range, apply antenna selection criteria by selecting an antenna configuration that supports the assigned frequency band and range requirements per MCRP 3-40.3C.
  • ELO-182: Given a list of frequencies, identify military radio frequency bands by classifying frequencies into HF, VHF, and UHF categories per MCRP 3-40.3C, Chapter 1.
  • ELO-183: Given various antenna types (e.g., Dipole, Whip, OE-254), describe antenna radiation patterns and range capabilities by matching antenna characteristics to mission distance requirements per MCRP 3-40.3C.
Body

Military Radio Frequency Bands

The electromagnetic spectrum is divided into bands that dictate how radio waves behave and what equipment is required.

  • High Frequency (HF): 3 to 30 MHz. Used for long-range communication via sky wave propagation.
  • Very High Frequency (VHF): 30 to 300 MHz. The primary band for MAGTF tactical ground communications, generally limited to line-of-sight.
  • Ultrahigh Frequency (UHF): 300 MHz to 3 GHz. Used for ground-to-air, satellite communications (SATCOM), and short-range line-of-sight.

Antenna Radiation Patterns and Range

Different antennas distribute energy in specific ways, which determines their effective range and application.

  • Omnidirectional (Whip): Radiates energy equally in all directions (360 degrees). Best for mobile operations and short-range VHF/UHF.
  • Bidirectional (Dipole): Radiates energy in two main directions. Ideal for established HF links at medium ranges.
  • Directional (OE-254/Log Periodic): Concentrates energy in a specific direction to increase range and reduce interference/detection.

Selection Criteria for Mission Success

To select the right antenna, the operator must balance the assigned frequency, the distance to the receiving station, and the tactical environment.

  • Short Range (0-30 miles): Typically VHF/UHF using whip or OE-254 antennas.
  • Medium to Long Range (30-300+ miles): Typically HF using NVIS (Near Vertical Incidence Skywave) or long-wire configurations.
  • Terrain Considerations: High ground is essential for VHF/UHF line-of-sight, while HF can overcome terrain obstacles using sky wave propagation.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are the RTO for a reconnaissance team. You are assigned a frequency of 4.500 MHz (HF) and must establish a link with a base 120 miles away located behind a mountain range. You have a manpack radio, a 10-foot whip antenna, and a field-expedient wire kit.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the frequency band (HF).
  2. Determine the propagation requirement (Sky wave/NVIS required due to distance and terrain).
  3. Evaluate the available antennas (Whip vs. Wire).
  4. Select the wire antenna and configure it as a Half-Wave Dipole to support the HF sky wave requirement.
  5. Verify the antenna length calculation based on the 4.500 MHz frequency.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the classification of HF, VHF, and UHF bands and how antenna types like the whip and dipole provide different radiation patterns to meet mission ranges. Understanding these criteria ensures the MAGTF maintains reliable command and control.

Closing Statement: The most powerful radio in the Marine Corps is useless if the energy never reaches the target. Master your antenna selection, and you master the airwaves.

Lesson 70: Antenna Polarization Selection

TLO: TLO-070

Introduction

Gain Attention: Have you ever had a radio check come back 'weak but readable' even though you were only a mile away from the other station? You might have had the best antenna and the right frequency, but if your antenna was standing straight up while the receiving antenna was laying flat, you were losing up to 95% of your signal strength. This is the 'cross-polarization' trap, and it is a common mistake that can jeopardize a mission.

Overview: This lesson defines antenna polarization and provides the criteria for selecting vertical or horizontal orientation based on the frequency band and the intended mode of propagation (ground wave vs. sky wave).

Objectives:

  • TLO-070: Given a tactical radio, a frequency, and a mission requirement, apply antenna polarization selection by matching the polarization (vertical, horizontal, or circular) to the frequency band and transmission mode per MCRP 3-40.3C.
  • ELO-184: Given a list of antenna types and MCRP 3-40.3C, define antenna polarization by identifying the physical orientation of the radiated electric field per MCRP 3-40.3C, page 2-6.
  • ELO-185: Given a tactical scenario involving ground wave and sky wave propagation, describe the advantages of vertical and horizontal polarization per MCRP 3-40.3C, pages 2-9 and 2-10.
  • ELO-186: Given various frequency bands (HF, VHF, UHF) and MCRP 3-40.3C, identify polarization requirements for various frequencies per MCRP 3-40.3C, page 2-8.
Body

Defining Polarization

Polarization is the orientation of the electric field (E-plane) as it leaves the antenna.

  • Vertical Polarization: The electric field is perpendicular to the Earth's surface (e.g., a standard whip antenna).
  • Horizontal Polarization: The electric field is parallel to the Earth's surface (e.g., a horizontal dipole).
  • Circular Polarization: The electric field rotates as it propagates; primarily used in SATCOM to overcome atmospheric rotation.

Advantages of Polarization Types

The choice of polarization affects how the signal interacts with the ground and the atmosphere.

  • Vertical Advantages: Best for ground wave communication (VHF). It is easier to employ on mobile platforms and provides omnidirectional coverage.
  • Horizontal Advantages: Best for HF sky wave (NVIS). It is less susceptible to man-made interference and provides better performance when communicating over long distances via the ionosphere.

Matching Polarization to Frequency and Mode

To ensure maximum signal transfer, the transmitting and receiving antennas must use the same polarization.

  • VHF/UHF Ground-to-Ground: Use Vertical polarization for standard tactical nets.
  • HF Sky Wave: Use Horizontal polarization to maximize reflection off the ionosphere.
  • SATCOM: Use Circular polarization to ensure the signal can be received regardless of the satellite's orientation.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are setting up a base station for an HF NVIS net to communicate with units 50-100 miles away. You are also monitoring a VHF convoy net on a separate radio.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify the propagation mode for the HF net (Sky wave/NVIS).
  2. Identify the propagation mode for the VHF net (Ground wave).
  3. Orient the HF Dipole antenna horizontally to support sky wave propagation.
  4. Orient the VHF whip antenna vertically to support ground wave communication with the convoy.
  5. Ensure all stations in the net are informed of the polarization to ensure matching.
Conclusion

Summary: Polarization is the physical orientation of the radio wave's electric field. We have learned that vertical polarization is the standard for VHF ground wave, while horizontal polarization is the preferred choice for HF sky wave operations.

Closing Statement: In the field, 'close enough' doesn't work for polarization. Match your orientation to your mission requirements to ensure your signal is heard loud and clear.

Lesson 71: Antenna Orientation and Azimuth

TLO: TLO-071

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine you are in a hide site, trying to send a critical SITREP. You have a perfect line of sight, but your signal is being drowned out by enemy jamming or local interference. Simply having a powerful radio isn't enough; if your antenna is pointed the wrong way, you are shouting into the wind while the enemy's noise fills your ears. Mastering antenna orientation is the difference between a clear transmission and total radio silence.

Overview: This lesson covers the principles of orienting directional antennas to maximize signal strength and minimize interference. We will define antenna azimuth, explore the relationship between orientation and signal-to-noise ratio, and practice calculating the correct azimuth for distant stations.

Objectives:

  • ELO-187: Define antenna azimuth
  • ELO-188: Explain the relationship between antenna orientation and signal-to-noise ratio
  • ELO-189: Determine the required azimuth for antenna orientation
Body

Antenna Azimuth Fundamentals

Azimuth is the horizontal angle measured clockwise from a north base line (true or magnetic north) to the direction of the antenna's radiation pattern. For a horizontal half-wave antenna, the maximum radiation occurs broadside to the wire.

  • Reference North: Always specify if using True North or Magnetic North based on your map and compass.
  • Radiation Pattern: Directional antennas do not radiate equally in all directions; the azimuth identifies the 'lobe' of maximum energy.
  • MCRP 3-40.3C Reference: Page 2-26.

Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) and Nulls

Proper orientation does two things simultaneously: it places the distant station in the antenna's maximum radiation lobe and places known interference sources in the antenna's 'nulls' (areas of minimum radiation).

  • SNR Maximization: Increasing the desired signal while decreasing background noise or jamming.
  • Null Placement: By rotating the antenna, an operator can 'dial out' interference coming from a specific direction.
  • MCRP 3-40.3C Reference: Page 2-27.

Calculating and Determining Azimuth

To communicate effectively, the operator must determine the exact direction to the distant station using map coordinates and then translate that to a physical heading for the antenna.

  • Map Work: Use the protractor to find the grid azimuth between your location and the distant station.
  • Conversion: Apply the G-M angle to convert grid azimuth to magnetic azimuth for use with a lensatic compass.
  • Tolerance: Standards require calculation within +/- 5 degrees for effective HF/VHF directional links.
Practical Application

Scenario: You are located at Grid 12S VF 1234 5678. You must establish a link with a distant station at Grid 12S VF 2234 6678. An enemy direction-finding unit is known to be operating 90 degrees offset from your intended path.

Practice Steps:

  1. Identify your location and the distant station location on the map.
  2. Calculate the grid azimuth to the distant station using a protractor.
  3. Convert the grid azimuth to a magnetic azimuth.
  4. Identify the 'null' points of your horizontal half-wave antenna.
  5. Physically orient the antenna wire so the broadside (maximum radiation) faces the distant station azimuth.
  6. Verify the orientation using a lensatic compass.
Conclusion

Summary: We have covered the definition of azimuth, the importance of SNR in marginal communication environments, and the technical steps to calculate antenna headings. Proper orientation ensures your signal reaches the target while minimizing the impact of interference.

Closing Statement: In the fleet, you won't always have the luxury of a perfect environment. Your ability to orient your antenna precisely is what will keep the command's common operational picture updated when the spectrum gets crowded.

Lesson 72: Antenna Grounding Systems

TLO: TLO-072

Introduction

Gain Attention: Every radio operator knows that an antenna needs to be 'up,' but many forget that for many systems, the ground is just as important as the wire in the air. Without a proper ground, you are essentially operating with only half of an antenna system. A poor ground leads to ground losses, reduced range, and potential safety hazards for the operator.

Overview: This lesson explains the theory behind grounded antennas, the various types of grounding systems available to Marines, and how to select the best method based on the terrain you encounter in the field.

Objectives:

  • ELO-190: Explain grounded antenna theory
  • ELO-191: Identify types of antenna grounds
  • ELO-192: Select the appropriate grounding method
Body

Grounded Antenna Theory

For many antenna types, the earth acts as a reflecting surface. A grounded antenna uses the earth as the other half of the circuit (the 'image' antenna). The efficiency of this reflection depends entirely on the soil's conductivity.

  • Image Theory: The ground creates a virtual reflection of the antenna, completing the radiation pattern.
  • Conductivity: High conductivity (moist soil) improves reflection; low conductivity (sand/rock) absorbs energy, causing 'ground loss.'
  • MCRP 3-40.3C Reference: Page 2-19.

Types of Antenna Grounds

There are three primary ways to establish a ground in the field: ground rods, counterpoises, and ground screens.

  • Ground Rods: Metal stakes driven into the earth to reach moist soil.
  • Counterpoise: A network of wires used when the earth itself is a poor conductor; it acts as an artificial ground.
  • Ground Screen: A mesh or radial system used to provide a highly reflective surface directly under the antenna.
  • MCRP 3-40.3C Reference: Pages 2-20 through 2-23.

Environmental Selection Criteria

The choice of grounding method is dictated by the terrain. You must adapt your grounding strategy to the soil conditions to maintain signal integrity.

  • Moist/Loam Soil: Standard ground rods are usually sufficient.
  • Sandy/Dry Soil: Requires a counterpoise or ground screen because the soil cannot conduct electricity effectively.
  • Rocky Terrain: Ground rods cannot be driven; a counterpoise is mandatory for safety and performance.
  • MCRP 3-40.3C Reference: Page 2-20.
Practical Application

Scenario: Your unit has moved into a desert environment characterized by high sand content and extremely low soil moisture. You are tasked with setting up a grounded vertical antenna for long-haul HF communications.

Practice Steps:

  1. Assess the soil condition (dry sand).
  2. Determine that a standard ground rod will be insufficient due to low conductivity.
  3. Select the counterpoise method as the appropriate grounding solution.
  4. Lay out the counterpoise radials in a star pattern centered at the antenna base.
  5. Connect the counterpoise to the radio's ground terminal.
  6. Ensure all connections are tight and free of corrosion.
Conclusion

Summary: We have discussed how the earth completes the antenna circuit, the different hardware used for grounding, and how to adapt your grounding technique to sandy, rocky, or moist environments.

Closing Statement: A Marine who understands grounding is a Marine who can communicate from anywhere. Don't let poor soil conditions be the reason your message doesn't get through.

Lesson 73: Implementing Tactical Single-Channel Radio Antennas

TLO: TLO-073

Introduction

Gain Attention: Imagine your unit is pinned down in a 'dead space' where your standard vehicle whip antenna cannot reach the Combat Operations Center. You have the radio, but the terrain is winning. In this moment, your ability to transform a few feet of copper wire and a handful of insulators into a high-performance antenna is the only thing that will get the Quick Reaction Force to your position. Field-expedient antenna construction is not just a technical skill; it is a survival skill for the tactical communicator.

Overview: This lesson covers the technical requirements for calculating antenna length and the physical construction of field-expedient wire antennas to optimize signal strength in marginal environments.

Objectives:

  • TLO-073: Implement tactical single-channel radio (SCR) antennas.
  • ELO-193: Calculate the physical length of a half-wave dipole antenna.
  • ELO-194: Construct a field-expedient wire antenna.
Body

Calculating Antenna Length for Resonance

To ensure maximum power transfer, an antenna must be resonant at the operating frequency. For a half-wave dipole, the physical length is determined by the speed of light and the effects of end-capacitance in wire.

  • Standard Formula: Length in feet = 468 / Frequency in MHz.
